books.title: Extreme Animals
books.art_why: The book describes real animals that exist today, so photographs are appropriate.

pages.text: Have you noticed that some animals will go to extremes to be noticed? These oddest of creatures come in all sizes and shapes. Some walk in a funny way. Others eat strange things. Some wear bold, bright patterns to blend in. In this book, you’ll read about the largest and the smallest. You’ll learn about the loudest and the quietest. Check out these fun facts about some of the most remarkable animals in the world! A long-necked giraffe has extra long legs that make it as tall as a two-story house. An elephant can be over 4.5 meters (15 ft) tall and weigh as much as two big pickup trucks. The gigantic blue whale is the biggest creature. It’s as long as half of a football field. Biggest.
pages.brief: A long-necked giraffe stands on extra-long legs, as tall as a two-story house. An elephant, over 4.5 metres tall and heavy as two big pickup trucks, stands nearby. The gigantic blue whale swims in the ocean, as long as half a football field.

pages.text: Smallest A bee hummingbird is only 5 centimeters (2 in) long and weighs less than a spoonful of water. A Chihuahua is the smallest dog. It can ride along in your pocket. The tarsier, a tiny monkey with big eyes, is as small as a mouse. A giraffe hardly makes a sound. It has a voice, it just doesn’t use it much. A howler monkey screams to claim its territory and food supply. It can be heard from 8 kilometers (5 mi) away. A blue whale’s cry is as loud as a rocket taking off. It can be heard over long distances in the ocean. Quietest Loudest.
pages.brief: A tiny bee hummingbird, only 5 centimetres long, hovers near a spoonful of water. A Chihuahua small enough to ride in a pocket stands beside a tarsier, a tiny big-eyed monkey as small as a mouse. A howler monkey screams in the forest; a blue whale cries in the ocean.

pages.text: Longest Life Shortest Life A big land turtle can wander around, visiting in its neighborhood for 150 years. A mayfly has to do everything quickly. It only lives for one day after it hatches from its egg. Slowest A garden snail crawls so slowly that it doesn’t even look as though it’s moving! One type of falcon is able to dive through the air at 322 kilometers per hour (200 mph). A wild cheetah can chase after its lunch at over 105 kilometers per hour (65 mph). The long, strong legs of an ostrich help it to run as fast as a racehorse. Fastest.
pages.brief: A big land turtle wanders its neighbourhood. A mayfly rests just after hatching from its egg, living only one day. A garden snail crawls so slowly it hardly seems to move. A falcon dives through the air; a wild cheetah chases its lunch; an ostrich runs fast with long, strong legs.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Reptiles A snake’s eyes look as if they are always open and watching. Its eyelids are transparent, so you can’t see that they’re closed. If a lizard is caught by the tail, its tail will break off—but it can grow a new one. A hidden crocodile can hold its breath underwater for an hour. A type of lungfish can live for four years without food or water if it has to. Sea horse babies live safely in their father’s body until they are big enough to be on their own. A humpback whale’s big tongue weighs as much as a small car. Fun Facts About Water Creatures.
pages.brief: A snake's eyes look always open, its transparent eyelids closed. A lizard caught by the tail breaks it off and grows a new one. A hidden crocodile holds its breath underwater. A lungfish lives without food or water. Sea horse babies live safely in their father's body. A humpback whale's big tongue weighs as much as a small car.

pages.text: A halibut is a big, flat fish that has both eyes on the same side of its head. A camel can close its nose to keep the desert sand from blowing in. Every zebra has its own pattern of stripes. No two zebras are striped the same. A mudskipper is an odd fish that can jump out of the water, skip across mud, and climb a tree. A big, heavy hippo looks slow, but it can run faster than a person. Fun Facts About Mammals A kangaroo can balance on its tail and fight or punch with all four feet.
pages.brief: A halibut has both eyes on one side of its head. A camel closes its nose against desert sand. Every zebra has its own stripe pattern. A mudskipper jumps from water, skips across mud and climbs a tree. A heavy hippo runs faster than a person. A kangaroo balances on its tail and punches with all four feet.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Insects A butterfly chooses its lunch with its feet. It has little sensors on its feet that can taste flavors that it likes. A cricket’s ears are on its knees, not on its head. To hear better, it turns its knees toward the direction of the sound. An ant can find your picnic lunch. It has a sense of smell that’s as good as a dog’s. An ostrich is an odd bird for many reasons. Its brain is very tiny. Its eyes are huge and its neck is extra long. It swallows small rocks to help grind up its food. A speedy little hummingbird is the only bird that can fly backward. An eagle’s very light bones are hollow to help it fly. Its feathers weigh more than its bones do. Fun Facts About Birds.
pages.brief: A butterfly tastes its lunch with sensors on its feet. A cricket's ears are on its knees, turned toward sound. An ant can smell a picnic lunch as well as a dog. An ostrich has a tiny brain, huge eyes, a long neck, and swallows small rocks. A hummingbird flies backward. An eagle's hollow bones are lighter than its feathers.

pages.text: More Fun Facts About Birds A penguin is a bird that can swim or walk for many miles—but is unable to fly. The feathers of a flamingo are pink because of the nutrients in the tiny shrimp it eats. Extreme animals come in many sizes and shapes. You may have seen some of these animals before. Others may be new to you. These are some of the most extreme animals in the world! What other extreme animals do you know? Conclusion.
pages.brief: A penguin swims and walks many miles, unable to fly. A flamingo stands with pink feathers, coloured by the tiny shrimp it eats. Together they represent extreme animals that come in many sizes and shapes, a reminder to think about other extreme animals in the world.

books.title: Ships and Boats
books.art_why: The book spans ancient boats, Vikings and early explorers, times before photographs.

pages.text: Introduction Before there were cars, trains, or airplanes, boats were the fastest way to travel. They helped to shape history, leading explorers to new lands and spreading new ideas around the world. Ships and boats have changed a lot over the years but still have much in common with the earliest designs.
pages.brief: An explorer stands in a wooden boat on open water, looking toward a distant coastline. A second, more modern boat floats nearby, showing how ships have changed over the years while still sharing the same basic shape on the water.

pages.text: Early Ships and Boats The first boats were carved from single wooden logs. These dugout canoes were used in rivers, lakes, and oceans around the world. People used long poles, paddles, or oars to move the canoes through the water. Paddles and oars are long pieces of wood with broad, flat ends. They push against the water to move the boat forward. Later, people began to make boats with wooden frames. They covered the frame with bark, reeds, or animal skins to keep out the water.
pages.brief: Two people paddle a dugout canoe carved from a single log along a river. One uses a long pole while the other pulls a broad-ended paddle. On the shore, a wooden frame boat covered with bark, reeds, and animal skins rests beside the water.

pages.text: In the South Pacific, people were building boats that could sail well beyond the islands where they lived. People took two canoes and connected them using large wooden poles. This style of boat was called a catamaran. The catamaran could travel very fast. It also allowed safe travel from one island to another.
pages.brief: People guide a catamaran across open water between two South Pacific islands. Two canoes are joined by large wooden poles, and the boat moves fast over the waves. The island shoreline waits in the distance.

pages.text: Some frame ships, such as galleys, were much larger than log boats. Thousands of years ago, many groups of people around the Mediterranean Sea used galleys for trade and warfare. Galleys were frame ships covered with wood that carried many rowers. The largest galleys had hundreds of rowers sitting on several decks. Many galleys also had sails made from strong cloth. Sails could be used when the wind was blowing in the direction the ship was traveling.
pages.brief: A large wooden galley sails on the Mediterranean Sea. Rowers sit on several decks, pulling long oars, while a strong cloth sail rises above them. The frame ship is covered with wood and carries many people for trade and warfare.

pages.text: In time, boats and ships relied more and more on wind power. Sailboats could travel much farther than ships that relied on rowers for their power. The Vikings used wooden-framed longships to cross the sea to raid towns and villages on other coasts. Like galleys, longships had sails as well as oars. The Vikings could land by surprise anywhere along the coast, something that helped them in battle.
pages.brief: A Viking longship with a broad sail and rows of oars crosses the sea toward a coastal town. Vikings aboard prepare to land by surprise on the shore, ready to raid the town and villages along the coast.

pages.text: Around 500 years ago, larger sailing ships began to be built. These sailing ships were able to cross the ocean. Famous explorers such as Ferdinand Magellan used sailing ships to travel from Europe to North and South America. Magellan was also the first captain to sail completely around the world.
pages.brief: A large sailing ship with tall masts crosses the open ocean. An explorer on deck looks ahead as the ship travels from Europe toward the coast of South or North America. The vessel is built to cross the ocean.

pages.text: Modern Ships and Boats When steam engines were invented, they were used in many boat and ship designs. Steamships did not depend on the wind for power. They could sail into the wind or even when there was no wind at all. Steamboats using paddlewheels became an important way to move quickly up and down rivers.
pages.brief: A steamboat with a large paddlewheel moves along a river. The paddlewheel turns at the back, pushing the boat forward. A steamship on the water shows travel without depending on the wind.

pages.text: Today, many boats are made of metal and plastic. Many ships and boats use electricity to turn their propellers. The propellers push the boat through the water. Some modern ships are very large. Cruise ships are like floating hotels. They can carry thousands of people all around the world. Huge tankers carry oil and gas over the ocean.
pages.brief: A huge cruise ship with many decks sails on the ocean like a floating hotel, carrying thousands of people. Nearby, a massive tanker carries oil and gas across the water. Both modern ships are made of metal and plastic.

pages.text: Some boats and ships are built to do special work. Tugboats push and pull larger ships in places where they can’t move themselves. Fireboats help put out fires on other ships. Ferryboats carry cars and people.
pages.brief: A tugboat pushes a larger ship through a harbor. A fireboat sprays water onto a fire on another ship, while a ferryboat carries cars and people across the water. Each boat is built for special work.

pages.text: Many countries use ships and boats, large and small, to defend their coasts. Submarines hide under the surface of the water. Aircraft carriers serve as floating runways and allow planes and helicopters to fly anywhere in the world.
pages.brief: A submarine hides just under the surface of the water near a coast. An aircraft carrier serves as a floating runway, with planes and a helicopter on its deck, ready to fly anywhere in the world.

pages.text: Although large, modern boats with propellers are everywhere today, people still use smaller boats for fishing, fun, and sport. It is almost impossible to look at a river, lake, or ocean and not see a variety of boats. Many smaller boats still use paddles, oars, or sails, just as the earliest boats did.
pages.brief: On a lake, several small boats are used for fishing, fun, and sport. One person fishes from a rowboat, another paddles, and a sailboat moves nearby. People still use paddles, oars, and sails, just as the earliest boats did.

pages.text: Conclusion Ships and boats have played an important part in human history. For thousands of years, they have allowed people to explore their world. They are still an important way to move quickly over the water.
pages.brief: An early wooden boat and a sleek modern boat travel on open water, with a distant coastline ahead. For thousands of years, ships and boats have carried people to explore their world and move quickly over the water.

books.title: Weird Bird Beaks
books.art_why: Real birds and real habitats can be photographed for this factual nature book.

pages.text: Bearded Barbet I have a large, thick beak that has pointed parts on the bottom like sharp teeth. Hairlike feathers look like a beard on my beak. I live where it is dry in Africa, where I build my nest in a dead tree. I feed on fruit and sometimes on insects.
pages.brief: A bearded barbet perches in a dry African setting beside a dead tree. Its large, thick beak has pointed, tooth-like parts along the bottom and hairlike feathers that look like a beard. The bird holds fruit and a small insect, showing what it feeds on.

pages.text: Crossbill My beak is crossed like an X, which helps me to pull the seeds out of a pinecone. Pinecones grow on trees called conifers, but conifers don’t produce good pinecones every year. I travel all over to find pinecones instead of living in one place.
pages.brief: A crossbill clings to a conifer branch and pulls seeds from a pinecone with its crossed, X-shaped beak. More conifer trees stand around it in a landscape where it travels from place to place to find pinecones.

pages.text: Rhinoceros Hornbill I have a horn on the top of my beak that I use to knock down fruit. I also use my horn to fight and sometimes to attract a mate. I bring food to my mate when she sits on our eggs. If you think my horn looks weird, you should see my eyelashes! I am one of the few birds that have them.
pages.brief: A rhinoceros hornbill shows the horn on top of its beak and its unusual eyelashes. It knocks fruit down from a branch and carries food toward a mate sitting on eggs. Its strong horn is also used for fighting and for attracting a mate.

pages.text: Huia We are huias (HOO-yuhs). We lived in New Zealand until we became extinct. “I am the male. My beak is thick and strong.” “I am the female. My beak is thin and curved.” Our beaks are so different that for a long time, people thought we were completely different types of birds.
pages.brief: A male and a female huia stand together in New Zealand. The male has a thick, strong beak, while the female has a thin, curved beak. The two birds look very different, though they are the same kind of bird.

pages.text: Sword-Billed Hummingbird I am a very small bird with a very long beak. I’m the only bird with a bill that is longer than my body! I use my long beak and even longer tongue to get nectar from tube- shaped flowers. I can stick my tongue out and pull it back in again about 13 times per second!
pages.brief: A tiny sword-billed hummingbird hovers beside a tube-shaped flower. Its bill is longer than its whole body. The hummingbird has its long tongue stretched out to reach nectar, and the scene shows it flicking its tongue in and out very fast.

pages.text: Brown Pelican I have a pouch of skin under my beak that can hold a lot of fish. I hunt in the ocean, diving down from the air. I sometimes steal fish from other birds, but they steal from me, too. Gulls even sit on my head and back while they take fish right out of my pouch!
pages.brief: A brown pelican floats on the ocean with a pouch of skin under its beak stretched full of fish. It has dived down from the air to hunt. Gulls sit on the pelican’s head and back, taking fish right out of the pouch.

pages.text: Shoebill Stork My beak is shaped like a shoe with a hook on the end that helps me eat fish. Sometimes, I’ll eat frogs and even small crocodiles. I hunt fish by waiting for one to swim by and then falling onto it with my mouth open.
pages.brief: A shoebill stork stands in a wetland with its shoe-shaped beak and hooked tip. It waits for a fish to swim by, then falls onto it with its mouth open. A frog and a small crocodile are nearby as other possible food.

pages.text: Spoonbill I have a long beak that flattens out at the end like a spoon. Because I am white and pink, people sometimes think I’m a flamingo. To find food, I sweep my beak back and forth in the mud and shallow water. I like to eat frogs, shellfish, seaweed, and small fish.
pages.brief: A spoonbill stands in shallow water and mud, sweeping its long, spoon-shaped beak back and forth to find food. Its feathers are white and pink. Small fish, shellfish, seaweed, and a frog are shown in the water and mud around it.

pages.text: Toucan My huge and colorful beak is actually very light because it’s full of air pockets. I eat fruit, seeds, insects, and eggs. My beak helps me to reach fruit while I sit in rainforest trees. I have two claws that point forward and two that point backward to help me hold onto branches.
pages.brief: A toucan sits on a rainforest tree branch, reaching for fruit with its huge, colorful beak. The beak looks heavy but is full of air pockets and very light. Two claws point forward and two point backward as the bird grips the branch.

pages.text: Many of us have weird beaks. Sometimes they help us to catch or eat food. Sometimes they just look wild!
pages.brief: Many birds with strange and wild-looking beaks are gathered together. Some use their beaks to catch or eat food, while others simply show off their odd shapes. The group includes several different birds with unusual beaks, all with very different bill shapes.

books.title: Elephants
books.art_why: Elephants are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: The Largest Land Animal Did you know that elephants are the largest land animals in the world? I saw an amazing picture of a mother elephant with her baby. I wanted to learn more about elephants, so I checked out a book from the library. I learned many unusual facts about elephants that I can share with you.
pages.brief: A large mother elephant stands beside her small baby elephant in an open grassy place, photographed in the wild. In the foreground a young reader holds an open library book about elephants, looking closely at the picture. The child sits at a table with other books nearby.

pages.text: Elephant Bodies If you’ve ever seen an elephant in a zoo, you know they are huge. An adult male can weigh as much as six cars. I definitely don’t want an elephant to sit on me! Elephants have heavy gray bodies, thick legs, wrinkled skin, and floppy ears. Many elephants also have a pair of tusks, which are long, pointed teeth. Elephants use their tusks to peel the bark off trees and to dig for minerals. Do You Know? Elephants have the largest ears of any animal. They use their ears to hear, swat insects, cool off, and show their feelings.
pages.brief: A huge adult male elephant stands in a zoo enclosure, its heavy gray body, thick legs, wrinkled skin and floppy ears filling the frame. Its long pointed tusks press against a tree trunk as it peels away bark. Its large ears fan out widely.

pages.text: One really interesting part of an elephant is its long trunk. An elephant’s trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together into a special shape. An elephant can use its trunk like a hand to pick up food or other objects. The trunk works like a hose when an elephant drinks water or gives itself a shower. A trunk can even work like a snorkel, helping an elephant breathe underwater. Do You Know? An elephant’s trunk has no bones, but it has thousands of muscles. An elephant can lift a tree or pick a flower with its trunk.
pages.brief: A close view shows an elephant's long trunk curling around a small flower, lifting it gently. The elephant stands near water, its trunk stretched forward. In the background another elephant sprays water over its back with its trunk, cooling off.

pages.text: I read about two kinds of elephants. One kind lives in Africa, and the other kind lives in Asia. Here’s what I learned about their differences. African Elephants Asian Elephants bigger smaller thinner body rounder body big ears that cover shoulders smaller ears that do not cover shoulders trunk has two “fingers” trunk has one “finger” long tusks short tusks; some females have no tusks most live on grasslands live in forests.
pages.brief: An African elephant stands on open grassland, larger with big ears spread over its shoulders and a trunk with two finger-like tips. Nearby an Asian elephant stands among forest trees, smaller with a rounder body, smaller ears and one finger-like tip on its trunk.

pages.text: Elephant Families Elephants live in families of four to ten females and their young. The females, called cows, are all relatives—grandmothers, mothers, aunts, sisters, and daughters. A wise old female called the matriarch (MAY-tree-ark) is the leader of the family. She helps her family find food and water. She also keeps the family together and helps everyone stay safe.
pages.brief: A family group of several female elephants and their young stands together on a grassy plain. At the front, a wise old female matriarch lifts her trunk, leading the others. Grandmothers, mothers, aunts, sisters and daughters stand close around the calves.

pages.text: Male elephants stay with their mothers until they are about 11 years old—teenagers, in elephant years. Then they go to live with other males. Adult males, called bulls, often live alone except when they mate with females. Sometimes bulls use their tusks to fight each other for a female.
pages.brief: A young male elephant walks away from a family group toward two adult male elephants standing apart. The adult bulls face each other, lowering their heads and crossing tusks in a test of strength. The scene is open dry ground with sparse grass.

pages.text: Baby elephants, called calves, are incredibly cute! When a calf is born, everyone in the family strokes it with his or her trunk to welcome it. All the adults help care for the calves. If a calf gets stuck in the mud at a water hole, everyone helps pull it out. If a lion is near, the adults stand in a circle around all the calves to protect them. Do You Know? Baby elephants suck their trunks for comfort, just as young children sometimes suck their thumbs.
pages.brief: A newborn calf stands among adult elephants, each adult gently stroking the baby with its trunk. Nearby, a calf stuck in mud is being pulled out by several adults. In the background the adults form a protective circle around the calves.

pages.text: Food and Water Elephants are herbivores (UR-beh- vores), or plant eaters, and they like many kinds of food. They eat grass, leaves, bark, branches, fruit, flowers, and seeds. Elephants are always on the move, looking for food and water. They eat so much that they can’t stay in one place for very long. When they leave an area, the plants have time to grow back.
pages.brief: An elephant stands in a lush area, wrapping its trunk around a leafy branch and pulling leaves into its mouth. Around its feet are grasses, fallen fruit, flowers and seeds. The elephant is on the move, stepping forward as it searches for food and water.

pages.text: Sometimes three or more families of elephants join together to form a herd. A herd may travel together to look for food and water. Elephants often walk in single file with each family following its matriarch. They follow the same routes year after year as they move from place to place.
pages.brief: Several elephant families form a herd, walking in single file across a dusty trail. At the front a matriarch leads the way, with mothers and calves following close behind. More elephants stretch back along the same worn route, moving together toward food and water.

pages.text: Elephants need to drink water, just like people. Because they live in hot places, they also need water to cool off. Elephants like to give themselves showers. They also like to roll in mud or cover themselves with dust. Elephant skin may look tough, but it’s really very sensitive. Mud and dust help protect an elephant’s skin from insect bites and the Sun’s heat. This elephant is giving itself a dust shower.
pages.brief: An elephant stands in a hot, dry place, using its trunk to throw dust over its back. A second elephant rolls in thick mud nearby, coating its sensitive skin. Another sprays water over itself, cooling off. The scene shows elephants using water, mud and dust to protect their skin from insect bites and the sun's heat.

pages.text: Keeping Elephants Alive I was sad to learn that both kinds of elephants are endangered. Even though it is against the law, people kill elephants for their tusks. The tusks are made of ivory, which people use to make jewelry and pieces of art. People also change a lot of wild land into farms, which leaves some elephants with no place to live.
pages.brief: An elephant stands at the edge of wild land, its long tusks visible. Nearby, a cleared field shows where wild land has been turned into a farm. On a table in the foreground, carved ivory jewelry and art pieces are displayed.

pages.text: Many people around the world are trying to save elephants. Some countries have created special parks to protect elephants. Hunters are less likely to kill elephants that live in the parks than ones that live in the wild. Elephants are amazing animals. I hope people can help these gentle giants stay alive for a very long time.
pages.brief: Elephants walk safely inside a special park, a wide open space with grass and trees. A boundary fence separates the park from wild land beyond. In the distance, a small group of people watch the elephants, showing that many people around the world want to protect them.

books.title: Bedbugs Bite!
books.art_why: Bedbugs, homes, cities, dogs and suitcases exist today, so photographs are possible.

pages.text: Introduction Good night. Sleep tight. Don’t let the bedbugs bite! These words were just an old rhyme a few years ago. Bedbugs (or “bed bugs”) were hard to find. But today these words are good advice. Bedbugs have returned. These little pests are causing big problems in cities all over the world.
pages.brief: A dark bedroom at night with a bed and headboard, while several small brown bedbugs crawl near the mattress. Through a window, city buildings are visible, suggesting bedbugs causing problems in cities all over the world. The quiet room matches an old nighttime rhyme.

pages.text: What Are Bedbugs? Bedbugs are brown, crawling insects that grow to be about the size of apple seeds. They hide in tight spaces during the day and are active at night. As their name suggests, bedbugs often live in people’s beds. They might be hiding under your mattress. Bedbugs bite people or other animals to drink their blood.
pages.brief: A close-up of a brown bedbug, small as an apple seed, crawling on a mattress. Others hide in a tight crack during the day. At night, a bedbug bites a person’s arm to drink blood, and another bites a nearby animal.

pages.text: Bedbugs are not attracted to dirt or garbage. They don’t care if their hiding spots are fancy or plain. People who keep their homes clean can get them. People with a lot of money or a little money can get them. Even movie stars get bedbugs!
pages.brief: A clean bedroom with no dirt or garbage still has bedbugs hiding near the bed. Beside it, a plain room shows the same. A wealthy person, a person with little money and a movie star each stand in their own setting, showing bedbugs do not care who people are.

pages.text: Unlike mosquitoes, which fly around to find their meals, bedbugs like the easy life. They bite when a person is quiet and still. Their victims may be sleeping in bed or sitting quietly, watching TV.
pages.brief: A mosquito flies through the air while a bedbug crawls slowly nearby. In one room, a person lies still and asleep in bed as a bedbug bites. In another room, a person sits quietly while watching television, with a bedbug approaching.

pages.text: Bedbug Life Cycle It doesn’t take very long for a few bedbugs to become a lot of bedbugs. A female bedbug can lay more than two hundred eggs in her lifetime. The eggs hatch in six to ten days. When a bedbug eats, its body swells up. As it digests its food, its body shrinks. As a bedbug grows up, its outer skin becomes too tight for its body. When this happens, the bug molts, or sheds, its outer skin. A bedbug molts five times before it is an adult. A developing bedbug can go for months without eating. An adult bedbug can go for a year without food. But if a bedbug lives near people, it will eat every day.
pages.brief: A female bedbug lays more than two hundred tiny eggs in a hidden crack. Nearby, tiny young bedbugs hatch and gather. One bedbug’s body swells after eating, then shrinks as it digests. Another molts, shedding tight outer skin. A bedbug waits months without food near people.

pages.text: Bedbug Life Cycle Bedbugs shed their skins five times as they grow into adults. It usually takes bedbugs three to seven weeks to become adults.
pages.brief: A sequence of bedbugs at different growth stages, each leaving behind a shed outer skin on a dark surface. Five cast-off skins lie in a row, showing the bug molted five times. The final bedbug is fully grown, representing three to seven weeks of development.

pages.text: Cities with the most bedbugs Bedbugs have been reported in hundreds of cities across the United States and Canada. The following cities (listed alphabetically) have the most complaints about bedbugs. 1 Boston, MA 7 Denver, CO c New York, NY 2 Chicago, IL 8 Detroit, MI d Philadelphia, PA 3 Cincinnati, OH 9 Indianapolis, IN e San Francisco, CA 4 Cleveland, OH 0 Los Angeles, CA f Toronto, ON 5 Columbus, OH a Louisville, KY g Vancouver, BC 6 Dayton, OH b Minneapolis, MN h Washington, D.C. World Travelers Bedbugs can’t fly. They only walk as fast as ladybugs. But these little critters travel all over the world. How do they do it? They sneak rides with people who are traveling.
pages.brief: A map of the United States and Canada with many city locations highlighted, showing places with the most bedbug complaints. Small brown bedbugs crawl near a ladybug, showing they walk rather than fly. Nearby, a traveler with luggage suggests bedbugs sneaking rides with people traveling around the world.

pages.text: A suitcase or moving box makes a good hiding spot for a bedbug. If a family brings that suitcase to a hotel, the bugs may crawl out. Some of the bedbugs might find hiding spots in the hotel. Some might hide in another person’s suitcase and go home with them. Once they get to a new home, bedbugs travel from room to room by squeezing through tiny cracks in the walls or floors.
pages.brief: A suitcase and a moving box sit open in a hotel room, with bedbugs crawling out and hiding in small cracks. A family’s luggage is nearby, and one bedbug slips into another person’s suitcase. In a home, bedbugs squeeze through tiny cracks in a wall and floor to move from room to room.

pages.text: Getting Rid of Bedbugs It’s easy to spot bedbug bites. Many people get red, itchy bumps on their skin when they are bitten. But it’s not as easy to spot the bedbugs. They can hide in tiny places and only come out when it’s dark. But there are ways to find them.
pages.brief: A person’s arm shows red, itchy bumps from bedbug bites. Nearby, a bedbug hides in a tiny dark crack, hard to spot. The scene shows the difference between easy-to-see bites and bugs that stay hidden until dark.

pages.text: Bedbugs often leave clues that they are around. If you look closely, you may find shed skin and dark spots of dried excrement, or poop, near their hiding areas. But the best way to find them is to hire a special dog. Some dogs are trained to smell bedbugs. They sniff all over homes or hotel rooms. When they smell bedbugs, they place a paw on the spot. Once the bugs are discovered, people can get rid of them with steam or chemicals.
pages.brief: Near a bedbug hiding place, shed skin and dark spots of dried excrement are visible. A trained dog sniffs along a hotel room floor and places a paw on the spot where bedbugs hide. A person nearby prepares to treat the area with steam or chemicals.

pages.text: Conclusion Bedbugs are becoming common again in cities around the world. They are biting more people. Their bites don’t hurt, and they usually don’t spread germs or disease. But it’s still not nice to get them; they can itch—a lot. Things You Can Do: 1. Tell an adult if you find bites or other clues that bedbugs are nearby. 2. Wash your sheets, blankets, pillowcases, and bedspreads in hot water and dry them in a hot dryer. 3. Vacuum your mattress, bedframe, baseboards, and couches. 4. Wrap your mattress in a bedbug-proof mattress cover. 5. When staying in a hotel room, keep your clothes inside a closed suitcase and don’t leave the suitcase on the bed or the floor.
pages.brief: A person washes sheets, blankets and pillowcases in hot water and dries them in a hot dryer. Another vacuums a mattress, bedframe, baseboards and a couch. A mattress is wrapped in a bedbug-proof cover. In a hotel room, clothes stay inside a closed suitcase off the bed and floor.

pages.text: If you do get bedbug bites, try to not scratch them. They can get infected if they are scratched open. And remember, you are not alone. People all over the world get bedbug bites. That’s why for years people have said, “Good night. Sleep tight. Don’t let the bedbugs bite!”
pages.brief: A person with red bedbug bites on their arm tries not to scratch, while a small sore shows how scratching can infect skin. Around them, people in different parts of the world also have bedbug bites. The scene returns to a bedtime setting with the old nighttime rhyme in mind.

books.title: Watching Earth From Space
books.art_why: Satellites, the space station, storms and pollution are all real, photographable subjects today.

pages.text: Introduction The world around you has hills, trees, and buildings. Stand on the sidewalk. You will only see what is happening on your street. That is your normal view. Now imagine looking down at your town from space. You would have a much wider view. From space, you could see your entire country!
pages.brief: A child stands on a sidewalk in a town, with hills, trees and buildings all around. Above, a wide view looks down on the whole town from space, showing the entire country spread out far below.

pages.text: Scientists can study Earth from space. They use cameras on satellites that circle the Earth. The International Space Station is one satellite that has cameras.
pages.brief: Scientists at work studying Earth, while cameras on satellites circle the planet overhead. The International Space Station floats in orbit with cameras mounted on it, looking down at Earth.

pages.text: Pictures made by these cameras show changes that happen to Earth over time. These pictures record how the land changes. They show problems like pollution and climate changes.
pages.brief: Space camera pictures laid out side by side, showing the same land changing over time. The images record shifting land, polluted areas and signs of climate change, all captured from high above Earth.

pages.text: Weather Satellites Watch Storms Large storms can cause great damage. A storm warning system lets people know a dangerous storm is coming. However, not all areas have warning systems. People might not have time to escape a storm’s path. Satellite pictures help scientists predict where a storm will go. Then they can tell people to leave that area.
pages.brief: A large storm swirls over land, seen from a satellite. Scientists study the storm picture to predict where it will go, and people below leave their homes along the storm's path.

pages.text: Keeping Watch on Pollution Pictures from space can show where air or water is being polluted. For example, they can show where an oil spill is spreading. This information helps people who live nearby. It also helps with cleanup efforts. Satellite pictures record how long it takes for the environment to recover.
pages.brief: An oil spill spreads across the water, seen from space. People who live nearby watch the polluted water, and cleanup efforts begin on the shore as the environment slowly recovers.

pages.text: Air pollution can affect the health of large groups of people. Satellite pictures show where the dirty air starts. The pictures also show where the dirty air goes. For example, some overcrowded cities in China have very dirty air. There are many causes, such as burning coal for power. Pictures show the coal pollution drifting to other countries.
pages.brief: A crowded city in China sits under a thick layer of dirty air, with coal burning at a power plant. A satellite picture shows the polluted air drifting away toward other countries.

pages.text: Watching Changes to the Land Pictures from space show changes to land areas. For example, they show deforestation, or the loss of forests. They also show where land has worn away because of wind or water. The loss of rain forests is a major environmental concern. Rain forests help to clean our air. Deforestation is a world problem. Trees help keep our air clean. They are home to wildlife. Photos from space show large forest areas that have been cut down or burned.
pages.brief: A satellite view of a rain forest with large areas cut down and burned, bare ground where tall trees once stood. Remaining trees and wildlife stand beside the cleared patches.

pages.text: Deforestation is also a cause of land wearing away. That is because tree roots help to hold soil in place. Without tree roots, the soil slides away. Serious land loss has happened on the island of Madagascar. Entire forests have been cut down. People remove trees to use them or make space for new farmland. Photos show large amounts of soil being washed away and lost.
pages.brief: On the island of Madagascar, forests have been cut down and rain washes the bare soil away. Tree roots no longer hold the soil, so it slides off the land, leaving space for farmland.

pages.text: Watching Climate Change Effects Scientists say people are causing a lot of the changes in Earth’s climate. When we burn oil, coal, and natural gas we create gas in the air. This type of gas traps more heat than usual above Earth. Pictures from space show the effects of Earth becoming warmer. For example, they show where ice is melting or breaking apart.
pages.brief: A satellite picture of Earth shows ice melting and breaking apart into the sea. Below, oil, coal and natural gas burn, sending gas into the air that traps heat above the planet.

pages.text: Another result of Earth becoming warmer is the spread of deserts. Satellite pictures show where land is too dry. People can’t grow food or feed animals there. N 100 km Thinking Critically What types of laws do you feel would help to control pollution?
pages.brief: Dry, cracked land stretches out where deserts are spreading, seen from above. Nothing grows and no animals graze there, because the land is too dry for food or farming.

pages.text: Conclusion For most of history, people could see a small part of the world. They viewed everything at eye level. Even people who traveled could only see what was right in front of them.
pages.brief: A traveler walks along a road, seeing only what is right in front of them at eye level. Other people stand on the ground, viewing just a small part of the world around them.

pages.text: Today we can easily watch and track large areas of Earth. Pictures from satellite cameras tell us about Earth’s changes. They help us understand how changes happening far away might affect us. What we do with that knowledge may decide the future of our planet.
pages.brief: A wide satellite view of Earth on a screen, showing large areas of land tracked from above. People study the pictures to understand changes far away and what they mean for the planet's future.

books.title: Beyond the Five Senses
books.art_why: Science and nature concepts about real animals and human senses are shown with real-world subjects.

pages.text: Introduction Animals use senses to find food and stay out of danger. Our senses tell us what is happening with our bodies and in the world around us. You probably know about the five basic senses: hearing, sight, smell, touch, and taste. Did you know that animals can also have many other senses? Some of these senses are common to most animals. Others are rare and amazing.
pages.brief: A child stands outdoors with eyes open, ears alert, nose and hands ready, while nearby animals search for food and stay out of danger. The scene shows hearing, sight, smell, touch, and taste, and hints at other senses some animals share and some animals rarely have.

pages.text: Body-Position Sense Without looking, do you know where your left foot is right now? You can answer this question because your brain senses where your body parts are. Without this sense, an animal would not be able to move and do interesting things with its body.
pages.brief: A child stands on one leg with eyes closed, not looking at their left foot, and moves an arm and leg. A soft outline of the brain is shown sensing where each body part is, so the child can move and do interesting things with their body.

pages.text: Pain Sense Pain might seem as though it’s part of the sense of touch, but it isn’t. People and other animals can feel pain even when nothing is touching them. Pain helps us by letting us know that we’ve been hurt. It can also warn us to stop or change what we are doing before we get hurt.
pages.brief: A child holds a sore ankle with nothing touching it, face showing pain. Nearby, a dog stops running and changes direction. The scene shows that people and other animals can feel pain without contact, and that pain warns them to stop or change what they are doing.

pages.text: Sense of Balance Humans and many other animals have tubes inside their ears that give them a sense of balance. Other senses, such as sight and knowing where your body parts are, make balancing easier. That is why balancing is more difficult when your eyes are closed or your leg is “asleep.”
pages.brief: A child tries to balance on one leg with eyes closed and arms out. A cutaway view of the ear shows the tubes inside. Another child wobbles as if one leg is asleep, showing that sight and knowing where body parts are make balancing easier.

pages.text: Temperature Sense Sensing hot and cold is important for many animals. Some bats and snakes have special heat sensors that can help them find prey. A rattlesnake can “feel” the heat of a mouse’s body from over a foot away.
pages.brief: A rattlesnake rests on rocky ground and senses the body heat of a mouse more than a foot away. In the dark nearby, a bat also uses a special heat sensor. The scene shows how sensing hot and cold helps some animals find prey.

pages.text: Time Sense Scientists think humans have the best sense of time, but there’s a chance that other animals sense it, too. For example, dogs and cats sometimes seem to sense when it’s time for their owners to come home.
pages.brief: A dog and a cat wait near a home’s door, looking toward the road as if they sense their owner is about to come home. A clock shows time passing. The scene shows that dogs and cats sometimes seem to sense time, while humans are thought to have the best time sense.

pages.text: Using Sounds to “See” Some animals use sounds to “see” the things around them, even deep underwater or in the dark. By making sounds and listening to echoes, these animals can tell where things are. Some bats, dolphins, whales, and birds have this special sense.
pages.brief: A bat flies through a dark cave, a dolphin swims deep underwater, and a whale and a bird are in their own dark or underwater places. Each animal makes sounds and listens to echoes to tell where things are around it.

pages.text: Bonus-Color Vision Did you know that nature has more colors than the human eye can see? Some birds and insects can see those extra colors. Seeing extra colors helps these animals find food or attract mates.
pages.brief: A bird and an insect look toward flowers and fruit, with extra colors glowing around them that a nearby human cannot see. The bird searches for food, and the insect is drawn toward a mate. Nature has more colors than the human eye can see.

pages.text: Whisker Sense Whiskers on animals aren’t just cute. Whiskers help animals to sense movement in the air or water around them. Whiskers can also help animals squeeze through small spaces or catch other animals with their mouths.
pages.brief: A cat with long whiskers squeezes through a narrow gap, its whiskers bending as air moves around them. Underwater, a seal uses its whiskers to sense water movement and catch a fish with its mouth. The scene shows that whiskers are more than cute.

pages.text: Electric-Field Sense Every animal’s body gives off a weak electric field. Humans and most other animals can’t sense these fields, but some animals that live in water can. Some sharks can find fish hiding in the sand on the ocean floor just by using this sense.
pages.brief: A shark swims just above the sandy ocean floor. A fish hides in the sand below, giving off a weak electric field. The shark senses that field and turns toward the hidden fish, showing how some water animals can sense electric fields.

pages.text: Magnetic-Field Sense The needle in a compass always points north because of Earth’s magnetic field. Some animals have a kind of natural compass built into their bodies. These animals can always “feel” which way is north, so they can travel long distances without getting lost.
pages.brief: An animal travels across a wide landscape without getting lost. A compass needle points north, and faint magnetic field lines curve around Earth. The scene shows that some animals have a natural compass inside their bodies and can feel which way is north.

pages.text: Conclusion There are many senses beyond hearing, sight, smell, touch, and taste. As you explore the world, think about the extra senses that animals, including you, use every day.
pages.brief: A child explores outdoors, watching animals around them. The child and the animals use hearing, sight, smell, touch, and taste, along with extra senses, as they move through the world every day. The scene invites thinking about senses beyond the basic five.

books.title: What Lives in This Hole?
books.art_why: Real animals and real burrows can be photographed.

pages.text: Animal Burrows I found a big hole in the ground two months ago. I thought it might be an animal’s burrow. I took a picture with my phone to show my teacher.
pages.brief: A child kneels beside a big hole in the ground outdoors, holding a phone to take a picture of it to show a teacher later. The child found the hole and thinks it may be an animal’s burrow.

pages.text: She helped me find out what lives in the hole. Now I study the burrow of a different animal every week. Then I write about it on our class blog. Check out what I’ve learned!
pages.brief: A teacher helps a child learn about a burrow, and the child studies the burrow of a different animal every week. The child writes about each animal on a class blog to share what has been learned.

pages.text: Do You Know? Desert tortoise burrows can be very deep, but some are only a little bigger than the tortoise’s shell. Staying Cool A desert tortoise lives in this hole! This animal lives in a desert. It digs a burrow to get away from the heat. It spends most of its life in the burrow.
pages.brief: A desert tortoise lives in its burrow in a hot desert, using the hole to get away from the heat. Its burrow can be very deep, while another is only a little bigger than the tortoise’s shell.

pages.text: Wowser! The goliath bird-eating spider is the biggest spider in the world. Keeping Eggs Safe A huge spider lives in this hole! It lives in a deep burrow. A female lays about fifty eggs in a little bag. She takes the bag with her if she leaves to hunt.
pages.brief: A huge goliath bird-eating spider, the biggest spider in the world, sits in a deep burrow. The female carries a little bag holding about fifty eggs with her when she leaves the burrow to hunt.

pages.text: Making a Nest This hole belongs to puffins! These birds spend most of their life at sea. They use their strong wings and webbed feet to fly and swim. Puffins swim much better than they fly.
pages.brief: A puffin stands beside a burrow hole, while other puffins use strong wings and webbed feet to swim in the sea and fly above the water. These birds spend most of their life at sea and swim much better than they fly.

pages.text: Wowser! Adult Atlantic puffins have brightly colored bills at certain times of the year. Some people call these birds “sea parrots” or “clowns of the sea.” Puffins use a burrow as a nest. They dig the burrow on a high cliff near water. Both parents care for the egg and then the chick.
pages.brief: Two adult Atlantic puffins with brightly colored bills stand on a high cliff near the water beside a burrow nest. Both parents care for the egg and then the chick, and some people call these birds sea parrots or clowns of the sea.

pages.text: Living in the Dark Naked mole rats live in this hole! They spend their whole lives in the dark. They dig tunnels to find roots and other plant parts to eat.
pages.brief: Inside their dark underground tunnels, naked mole rats live and spend their whole lives in the dark. They dig through the soil, moving through the dirt to find roots and other plant parts to eat.

pages.text: Naked mole rats work together to build tunnels. One animal digs through soil at the front. Several others sweep dirt toward the back. An animal at the back kicks the dirt out of the tunnel.
pages.brief: Naked mole rats work together to build tunnels. One animal digs through the soil at the front, several others sweep dirt toward the back, and an animal at the back kicks the dirt out of the tunnel.

pages.text: Wowser! Japanese giant salamanders can grow as long as 1.5 meters (5 ft). Hiding and Laying Eggs A big salamander lives in this underwater hole! It lives in rivers and streams. It hides in a burrow or under rocks during the day. It comes out to hunt at night.
pages.brief: A big Japanese giant salamander, as long as 1.5 meters, hides in an underwater burrow or under rocks in a river or stream during the day. At night it comes out from hiding to hunt.

pages.text: In late summer, males and females gather at burrows. A female lays up to five hundred eggs there. A male watches the eggs to make sure fish don’t eat them.
pages.brief: In late summer, male and female giant salamanders gather at an underwater burrow. The female lays up to five hundred eggs there, and the male watches the eggs to make sure fish do not eat them.

pages.text: Wowser! A wombat’s burrow may be as long as three school buses! Taking a Nap A wombat lives in this hole! This animal digs a burrow with its huge claws. It sleeps in its burrow during the day. At night, it comes out to find plants to eat.
pages.brief: A wombat uses its huge claws to dig a long burrow that stretches as far as three school buses. It sleeps inside during the day, then comes out at night to find plants to eat.

pages.text: More to Come I’m going to study more animals that live in holes. Next, I will write about rabbits, snakes, and ants. It’s so fun to learn about animals!
pages.brief: A child watches a rabbit, a snake, and ants near their holes in the ground outside, planning to study more animals that live in holes and to write about these three next because it is so fun to learn.

books.title: Asthma
books.art_why: Real-world health topic with real people and medical devices.

pages.text: What Is Asthma? Asthma is a disease that makes it difficult for a person to breathe. When people breathe, air makes its way through the nose or mouth to the lungs. Air moves in and out of the lungs through special tubes.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a person’s head and chest shows the nose, mouth, lungs, and the special tubes that carry air. Air is shown moving from the nose and mouth down into the lungs, then flowing in and out through the branching tubes.

pages.text: On the right is a normal tube that carries air into and out of the lungs. On the left is one of these tubes during an asthma attack. These tubes swell and become narrow during an asthma attack. Because of this, less air moves into and out of the lungs. People with asthma might wheeze or cough. Their chest might feel tight. They may have a hard time breathing. A bad asthma attack can last for days or even cause death.
pages.brief: Two airways are compared side by side: a normal tube, open and clear, and an asthma-affected tube that is swollen and narrow. Beside them, a person presses a hand to a tight chest and coughs, showing wheezing, coughing, and difficult breathing during an attack.

pages.text: Asthma in the United States: 2001–2010 People with Asthma About 235 million children and adults around the world have asthma. Asthma can show up in a person at any age. About one child out of every ten in the United States has asthma. About half of these children will see their asthma get better as they grow older. However, their symptoms often return when they become older adults. One adult in twelve has asthma. Each year, more people in the United States and around the world get asthma.
pages.brief: A diverse crowd of children and adults fills a bright public space, representing people in the United States and around the world. Children of different ages stand among adults, suggesting how many people have asthma and how the number grows each year.

pages.text: Children Under Age 15 with Asthma in the United States: 2009 Doctors do not know how people get asthma. They do know that it cannot be passed from one person to another like a cold. However, the disease often runs in families. If both parents have asthma, their children are more likely to have it. People who are around cigarette smoke are also more likely to develop asthma.
pages.brief: A doctor sits with two parents and their child in a clinic, explaining asthma. The family listens closely. Nearby, cigarette smoke drifts from a lit cigarette, showing one risk factor. The scene suggests asthma often runs in families and is not passed like a cold.

pages.text: The Causes of Attacks Many things can cause asthma attacks. These triggers are different from person to person. Dust, animals, pollen, or mold can cause an attack for many people. Cigarette smoke, fumes from cars, and other strong smells are also common triggers. Coming down with a cold or the flu can often bring on an attack as well. Exercise can cause an asthma attack in some people.
pages.brief: A child stands in a dusty room near a cat, a dog, and a patch of mold, with pollen drifting from flowers outside. Cigarette smoke and car fumes drift through an open window, and the child holds a tissue from a cold. A bicycle nearby suggests exercise.

pages.text: Keeping Asthma Under Control Most people with asthma learn to control the disease. They often start by meeting with their doctor to create an action plan. Each person’s action plan is a little different. It can include a person’s triggers and how to avoid them. It can also include the kinds of medicines a person uses and how to use them correctly.
pages.brief: A doctor and a person with asthma sit together at a clinic table, going over a personal action plan drawn with simple pictures. The doctor points to steps for avoiding triggers and using medicines correctly while the person listens.

pages.text: People use different medicines to control asthma. Some people take pills every day. Others may take pills only when they feel the symptoms of asthma. Many people use inhalers. These devices spray a mist of medicine that is breathed in. Inhalers may be used daily or only when a person has an asthma attack.
pages.brief: A person holds an inhaler and breathes in a fine mist of medicine. Beside them, a small tray holds pills in two groups, showing daily pills and pills taken only when symptoms appear. The scene shows different ways people use medicine to control asthma.

pages.text: Do You Know? Some people use a nebulizer (NEB-yuh-ly-zer) to control asthma. Like inhalers, these machines deliver a mist of medicine that is breathed in. Unlike inhalers, these machines use power and can deliver larger amounts of medicine over a longer time.
pages.brief: A person sits calmly with a nebulizer mask over the nose and mouth. The nebulizer machine is plugged in and sends a mist of medicine through a tube to the mask, showing how it can deliver larger amounts over a longer time.

pages.text: Another important part of keeping asthma under control is staying healthy. Exercise, a healthy diet, and plenty of sleep can help keep asthma under control.
pages.brief: A person jogs outdoors in fresh air, then sits to a healthy meal of vegetables and fruit. Later, the same person sleeps peacefully in bed. The three scenes show exercise, a healthy diet, and plenty of sleep helping to keep asthma under control.

pages.text: Living with Asthma People with asthma can do anything that anyone else can. Many famous athletes have asthma. Jerome “The Bus” Bettis was fourteen when doctors told him he had asthma. It did not stop him from becoming a Super Bowl champion.
pages.brief: Jerome “The Bus” Bettis, a large football player in uniform, runs with the ball on a football field. A stadium crowd watches. He looks strong and determined, showing that asthma did not stop him from becoming a Super Bowl champion.

pages.text: Amy Van Dyken was an Olympic swimmer for the United States. She has asthma and won six gold medals. When she was a child, her doctor said that she should start swimming to make her lungs stronger.
pages.brief: Amy Van Dyken, an Olympic swimmer for the United States, stands beside a swimming pool in a swimsuit. Six gold medals are displayed nearby, and she smiles. The scene shows she has asthma and still won six gold medals, after her doctor recommended swimming to strengthen her lungs.

pages.text: People with asthma have climbed the tallest mountains. They have explored the deep waters of the ocean. They have led countries and made discoveries that have changed the world. With an action plan and a healthy lifestyle, asthma doesn’t have to slow anyone down.
pages.brief: A montage shows people with asthma doing extraordinary things: one climbs a snowy mountain peak, one dives deep underwater, one speaks as a country’s leader, and one studies a new discovery. Together they show that asthma does not have to slow anyone down.

books.title: Awesome Ants
books.art_why: The book includes ancient ants under dinosaurs, which cannot be photographed.

pages.text: A Little History You’ve seen them marching through grass and across sidewalks. You may have even seen them crawling over your kitchen counter. We’re talking about ants—tiny, strong, awesome ants.
pages.brief: Tiny ants march in a line through green grass and across a concrete sidewalk. Nearby, a few ants crawl over a kitchen counter. The small insects move together in an everyday outdoor and indoor setting, showing how easily people can see them.

pages.text: Ants are about 100 million years old. They were crawling around under the dinosaurs! Between then and now, they’ve changed a lot. Today, over 10,000 species of ants live on every continent except Antarctica. They have been able to survive so long because of their bodies and how they live.
pages.brief: Long ago, ants crawl on the ground beneath giant dinosaurs. Today, over 10,000 species of ants live on land across the world, and Antarctica is the only continent without them. The ants are tiny but have survived a very long time.

pages.text: Body Parts Like all insects, ants have six legs and three body parts. The back part of their body is the abdomen. This part holds the heart and stomachs. Some ants have stingers that they use to protect themselves. Their three pairs of legs attach to the middle part, called the thorax. Each leg has little hooks that allow ants to climb almost anything. Ants can even hear with their legs by feeling vibrations through the ground.
pages.brief: A close view of an ant shows six legs and three body parts. The abdomen at the back holds the heart and stomachs, and a stinger is visible. Three pairs of legs attach to the middle thorax, each leg with tiny hooks gripping a surface.

pages.text: The head contains the brain, two eyes, antennae, and jaws. The jaws open and close like scissors. They are used for cutting and carrying things. Ants can lift more than twenty times their own weight. Ants also have other mouthparts for chewing food and drinking.
pages.brief: An ant’s head is shown close up with two eyes, moving antennae, and scissor-like jaws. The jaws grip and carry a small piece of food. Other mouthparts are visible as the ant chews and drinks, and its strong body suggests it can lift many times its own weight.

pages.text: The two eyes are each made up of many smaller eyes. Even though ants have so many eyes, they can’t see very well. Instead, they use their antennae to get around. The antennae are like all-in-one sense machines. Ants use them to taste, smell, hear, and communicate with other ants through touching. The long, thin antennae are always moving around.
pages.brief: A close-up of an ant’s face shows two large eyes made of many smaller eyes and long, thin antennae moving through the air. The antennae touch the ground and nearby objects, sensing smells, tastes, sounds, and vibrations as the ant feels its way around.

pages.text: Let’s Talk Ants communicate with each other in three ways: touch, sound, and smell. Ants touch each other with their antennae in different ways to send different messages. They can also make noises to communicate by rubbing their legs together or on their bodies.
pages.brief: Two ants stand face to face and touch antennae to send a message. Another ant rubs its legs together against its body to make a sound. Around them, ants communicate by touch, sound, and smell in their busy group.

pages.text: The main way ants communicate is by smell. They release chemicals that other ants can smell long after the first ant is gone. Different smells send different messages. For example, a crushed ant releases chemicals that attract other ants. The chemicals also make the other ants attack anything nearby that might be a danger. An ant that has found food will lay down a trail of chemicals for other ants to follow. The trail allows them to find the food and return to the colony.
pages.brief: An ant lays a chemical trail from food back toward the colony, and other ants follow it. Nearby, a crushed ant releases a smell that attracts ants and makes them gather, ready to attack anything nearby that might be a danger.

pages.text: One Big, Happy Family Ant colonies are filled with activity. Usually built underground, they have many different rooms, which all have different uses. Some rooms store food, while others are used to care for the young. Colonies even have rooms for ants to relax in. This cast shows the upper part of a large ant colony. Scientists think this colony went over 12 meters (39 ft) into the ground.
pages.brief: A large ant colony is shown underground with many rooms and tunnels. Some rooms hold stored food, others contain young ants being cared for, and some are spaces where ants relax. The tunnels reach deep into the ground, showing the colony’s huge size.

pages.text: Within the colony, every ant has a job. Worker ants and soldier ants find food and protect the nest. These are usually the ants you see above the ground. Other ants build the nest, take care of the young, and do other jobs. All these ants are female, but only one is allowed to lay eggs: the queen. In other words, all the ants in a colony are related. What About the Boys? Male ants have only one purpose in most colonies: to mate with the queen. Once they’ve done their duty, most male ants simply die.
pages.brief: Inside and above the colony, worker ants and soldier ants find food and guard the nest. Other ants build tunnels and care for the young. The queen lays eggs while all the ants around her are female and related. A male ant is shown near the queen.

pages.text: The Queen The queen is the leader of the colony. The largest of all the ants, queens are egg-laying machines. Some queens can lay thousands of eggs every day. They can also live longer than most other insects— over twenty-five years. I Can Fly! Some young queens have wings that they use to fly off and start new colonies. The wings fall off when the queens start laying eggs. Some males can also fly. When they land near a colony, worker ants rip the wings off. Then they rush the male to the queen so the two can mate before the male dies.
pages.brief: A large queen ant, the biggest ant in the colony, stands at the center, surrounded by smaller worker ants. Some young queens and males have wings and fly away. Worker ants pull the wings off a landed male and hurry him toward the queen.

pages.text: Let’s Go Floating Not even water can stop some ants. They climb on top of each other and link their legs until they form a raft or bridge made of their own bodies. Yep, Ants Are Awesome Ants may be small, but they can do awesome things. Thousands or millions of ants working together can build bridges or float across rivers. They can overpower animals hundreds of times their own size for food.
pages.brief: Many ants climb on top of one another and link their legs to form a living raft on water and a bridge over a gap. A much larger animal is overwhelmed by swarming ants as they work together to get food.

pages.text: So the next time you come across a trail of ants, stop and watch or, better yet, follow them. When you see what these little gals are capable of, you’ll understand just how awesome they are.
pages.brief: A long trail of ants crosses the ground, moving together in a line. The tiny ants show their strength and teamwork as they continue on their way. The scene invites a close look at what these small insects can do.

books.title: Roadside Oddities
books.art_why: Roadside attractions and monuments exist in the real world today.

pages.text: What Is The Thing? Giant signs at the side of the road ask, “The Thing? What is it?” Roadside attractions such as The Thing are odd and wonderful. They ask people to stop and check them out.
pages.brief: At the side of a road, several giant signs stand near a highway. Travelers slow down and pull over to look at the odd roadside attraction. The signs are large and eye-catching, and people stop to check out what is there.

pages.text: World’s Largest Baseball Bat The world’s largest baseball bat is taller than the five- story building it stands beside. It weighs as much as three school buses.
pages.brief: A gigantic baseball bat stands upright beside a five-story building. It is taller than the building. The scene shows the world's largest baseball bat, making the ordinary building look small next to its enormous size.

pages.text: The Corn Palace The Corn Palace is decorated with grasses and corn of different colors. The Corn Palace is also the world’s largest bird feeder. When winter begins, the birds and squirrels eat the art!
pages.brief: A large palace building is decorated with grasses and corn in many different colors. In winter, birds and squirrels gather on the decorated walls and eat the art. The building is known as the world's largest bird feeder.

pages.text: Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum Do you have an extra toilet seat? Bring it to Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum. Barney Smith has made more than one thousand toilet seats into works of art.
pages.brief: Inside Barney Smith's Toilet Seat Art Museum, more than one thousand toilet seats are displayed as works of art. Barney Smith has transformed ordinary toilet seats into art pieces. A person with an extra toilet seat could bring it to the museum.

pages.text: A big elephant needs a big drink of water. Lucy the Elephant The world’s largest elephant is a six- story building you can climb inside!
pages.brief: A giant elephant building stands outdoors, six stories tall. It is the world's largest elephant. People climb inside it. A big elephant needs a big drink of water, so a large water source is near the giant elephant.

pages.text: Boll Weevil Monument A hundred years ago, a bug called the boll weevil destroyed cotton plants in Alabama. Farmers had to grow different plants. In the end, that helped the farmers. So they built a monument to the weevil.
pages.brief: A monument to a boll weevil stands in Alabama. A hundred years ago, the bug destroyed cotton plants, so farmers had to grow different plants. In the end, that helped the farmers, and they built this monument to the weevil.

pages.text: Sign Post Forest The Sign Post Forest isn’t made of trees. It’s made of more than 100,000 signs. Do You Know? Not all roadside attractions are made by people. General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park is the world’s largest tree. It is thought to be between 2,300 and 2,700 years old.
pages.brief: A dense forest of signs stands in place of trees, with more than 100,000 signs packed together. Nearby, the General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park rises as the world's largest tree. It is thought to be between 2,300 and 2,700 years old.

pages.text: Inset: Stonehenge is a ring of stones raised 4,000 to 5,000 years ago. It is 90 miles west of London. Carhenge In Nebraska, you can visit a model of England’s Stonehenge. It wasn’t built with old stones, but with thirty-eight old cars.
pages.brief: A ring of ancient standing stones forms Stonehenge in England, raised 4,000 to 5,000 years ago and located 90 miles west of London. In Nebraska, Carhenge is a model of Stonehenge made from thirty-eight old cars instead of old stones.

pages.text: London Bridge London Bridge started out in London, England. Then an American bought the bridge. He spent a lot of money to have the bridge moved to Arizona.
pages.brief: London Bridge stands in Arizona after starting out in London, England. An American bought the bridge and spent a lot of money to have it moved to Arizona. The stone bridge is shown in its new location.

pages.text: World’s Largest Basket Workers at a basket company get to work inside a basket that’s seven stories tall. When it was first built, a pilot flew his small plane through the handles!
pages.brief: Workers at a basket company work inside a basket building that is seven stories tall. The world's largest basket has huge handles. When it was first built, a pilot flew his small plane through the handles.

pages.brief: World's largest roadside objects stand in different places: a tire in Allen Park, Michigan; chest of drawers in High Point, North Carolina; violin on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia; artichoke in Castroville, California; ketchup bottle in Collinsville, Illinois; cuckoo clock in Sugarcreek, Ohio; ear of corn in Olivia, Minnesota; rubber stamp in Cleveland, Ohio.

pages.text: A Map to Amazement UNITED STATES MEXICO Stop and Look Roadside attractions grab people’s attention and cause them to stop. Do you want to know what The Thing is in Arizona? You’ll just have to pull off the road to find out!
pages.brief: A map shows the United States and Mexico, pointing to roadside attractions across the land. Roadside sights grab people's attention and cause travelers to stop. A driver on a road in Arizona pulls off to discover what The Thing is.

books.title: Coral Reefs
books.art_why: Coral reefs exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Coral Reefs.
pages.brief: A bright coral reef underwater, with varied coral shapes in clear blue water. Sunlight filters down from above onto the colorful reef. The scene focuses only on the reef itself, with no people, boats, fish or other animals visible.

pages.text: Underwater Communities Coral reefs are huge ocean communities. Millions of animals and sea plants live in them. Coral reefs are very busy places. Many kinds of coral make up reefs. Corals aren’t rocks or plants. They are tiny animals called polyps (PAH-lips). Most polyps are smaller than a pea.
pages.brief: A wide underwater coral reef crowded with many kinds of coral, sea plants and small sea animals. In the foreground, a close view of tiny coral polyps attached to the reef, each smaller than a pea. Clear blue water surrounds the busy community.

pages.text: Kinds of Coral There are two kinds of coral. The first kind is hard corals. These corals have hard skeletons. Over time, thousands of polyp skeletons help build a reef. Algae (AL-jee) live in the bodies of these corals. Algae are simple cousins of plants. The algae are food for the corals.
pages.brief: Hard corals on a reef, with hard, stony skeletons visible in clear water. A close view reveals tiny algae living inside the coral bodies, where the algae serve as food. Over time, thousands of polyp skeletons help build the reef.

pages.text: Soft corals are the second kind of coral. They often look like trees or other plants. These corals can bend with the water currents. Algae live in the bodies of some of them. Many corals are named for what they look like. Brain corals look like brains. Sea fans look like open fans. Sea pens look like old-fashioned pens made from big feathers.
pages.brief: Soft corals swaying in water currents, some looking like trees or other plants. Brain coral has rounded, brain-like ridges, a sea fan spreads open like a fan, and a sea pen looks like an old-fashioned feather pen. Tiny algae live inside some of these soft corals.

pages.text: A Busy Home Thousands of fish of all sizes, shapes, and colors live on reefs. They depend on the reef for food and safety. Shrimp, lobsters, crabs, and sea stars feed on reefs. The holes in reefs are good places for animals to hide.
pages.brief: A busy reef filled with thousands of fish in many sizes, shapes and colors. Shrimp, lobsters, crabs and sea stars feed among the corals, while small animals hide inside holes and crevices in the reef. Clear ocean water surrounds the crowded home.

pages.text: Where Corals Live Most coral reefs are close to shore in warm parts of the world. Corals need certain things to stay healthy. They need algae for food. They must be near the water’s surface so the algae can get enough sunlight. Also, both corals and algae need water that is not too warm or cold. There are three kinds of coral reefs. Fringing reefs are close to the shore.
pages.brief: A warm, shallow coral reef close to a shoreline, with sunlight reaching down through clear water. Corals and their algae live near the water's surface in water that is not too warm or cold. A fringing reef runs near the shore.

pages.text: Barrier reefs have a large, deep area of water between the reef and the shore. Wowser! The Great Barrier Reef is about half the size of Texas.
pages.brief: A barrier reef separated from the shore by a large, deep stretch of water. The reef rises in the ocean with the shoreline distant across the deep channel. The vast reef stretches far across the sea, suggesting the Great Barrier Reef, about half the size of Texas.

pages.text: Atolls, the third type of reef, are shaped like circles. They form around the edges of a slowly sinking island. After the island sinks, a small body of water called a lagoon forms in the center.
pages.brief: A ring-shaped atoll coral reef in the ocean, formed around the edges of a slowly sinking island. In the center, a small body of calm water called a lagoon lies inside the circle of reef. The low island edges sit near the water.

pages.text: Dangers to Coral Reefs Coral reefs are very fragile. Many things can harm them. People are the biggest cause of harm. People burn huge amounts of coal, oil, and gas to power cars and factories and to heat and cool buildings. Burning coal, oil, and gas is making Earth’s air and water warmer. Warmer ocean water causes many problems for coral reefs.
pages.brief: A fragile coral reef underwater, with corals looking stressed. Above the water, cars, factories and buildings show people burning coal, oil and gas. Warmer air and warmer ocean water surround the reef, showing how human activity causes problems for corals.

pages.text: Corals are getting sick. Coral diseases can destroy a big reef in just weeks. Warmer water is also causing corals to lose their algae. Without algae, corals have no food. They also lose their color and turn white. Three-fourths of all coral reefs have this problem.
pages.brief: A coral reef where many corals have turned white after losing their algae. Sick corals show pale, damaged patches, and the reef looks unhealthy. Warm water surrounds the corals, showing the problem that affects three-fourths of all coral reefs.

pages.text: Other things harm coral reefs, too. Some people use poisons and explosives when they fish. Boats can break off large pieces of reefs. Dirt and trash can smother them. Boats can also leak gas and oil. Gas and oil hurt coral, plants, and fish.
pages.brief: A coral reef harmed by people. A boat above leaks gas and oil into the water, broken pieces of coral lie below, and dirt and trash settle on the reef. Nearby, fishing with poisons or explosives damages coral, plants and fish in the surrounding water.

pages.text: Protecting Coral Reefs Coral reefs are beautiful. They are also important for many reasons. Reefs help protect coasts from storms and floods. They provide food for many kinds of fish that people eat. Some reef plants and animals are used for medicines. Many countries try to protect their reefs. They have written laws and rules to keep reefs safe. But people do not always follow those laws and rules.
pages.brief: A healthy coral reef beside a coastline, with fish swimming among colorful corals. The reef lies between the open ocean and the shore, helping protect the coast from storms and floods. Reef plants and animals that may be used for medicines grow on the reef.

pages.text: Half of the world’s reefs have been destroyed. Most of the others are in trouble. Scientists are working to help coral reefs. Each of us can help, too, even if we don’t live near an ocean. Never throw things in the water. Learn about what people do that makes ocean water too warm. We can all help protect coral reefs. Then all the living things on coral reefs will continue to have homes and food. Coral Nurseries Scientists can grow pieces of healthy coral in nurseries. The pieces may be rescued from boat-related damage or coastal building projects. Scientists hang the pieces from bars, place them in baskets, or attach them to stands on the ocean floor. They later move the pieces to damaged reefs to help fix them.
