pages.brief: Scientists in a coral nursery underwater hang pieces of healthy coral from bars, place them in baskets and attach them to stands on the ocean floor. Nearby, a damaged reef waits for the grown coral pieces to be moved there and help repair it. The reef shows areas that have been destroyed.

books.title: Wiggly Worms
books.art_why: Real earthworms, soil, farm animals, and worm farms can be photographed.

pages.text: orms Wiggly Worms.
pages.brief: Several earthworms wiggle through dark, moist soil, their long bodies bending and stretching. One worm curls near the surface while others weave between small clumps of dirt. The scene is close-up, showing only worms and soil.

pages.text: orms iggly orms.
pages.brief: A close-up view shows two earthworms wiggling through rich, dark soil. Their bodies curve and stretch in different directions, one looping over a clump of dirt and the other sliding past it. Small grains of soil press around them.

pages.text: Small Animals, Big Changes What do you know about earthworms? These small animals change the soil in big ways.
pages.brief: An earthworm tunnels through dark, crumbly soil, its body curved as it pushes through. Around it, tiny grains of soil shift and mix. The worm is small compared with the wide patch of soil, showing how one small animal changes the ground.

pages.text: Earthworm Bodies An earthworm’s body is shaped like one tube wrapped around the outside of another tube. On the outside is a tube of muscle, and on the inside is a tube that breaks down food.
pages.brief: A close-up, realistic view of an earthworm stretched across moist soil shows its long, tube-shaped outer body. Inside the body, a narrower inner tube is visible, suggesting the food passage. The worm’s outer muscle tube wraps around the inner tube.

pages.text: The body of an earthworm is made up of many parts. Each part is shaped like a ring, and it can bend and stretch. Earthworm Facts Common names Earthworm, night crawler Animal group Invertebrate (no backbone) Life span Up to 6 years Size (common species) 3½–12 inches (9–30 cm) Habitat All types except deserts and areas where the ground is always frozen; prefer moist, rich soil.
pages.brief: A close-up photo of an earthworm on moist soil shows its body divided into many ring-shaped segments. The worm bends and stretches, with some rings squeezed close and others spread apart. Its body curves gently over a small clump of dirt.

pages.text: Earthworms move by stretching out their bodies and pulling themselves forward. Short, tough hairs on earthworms’ bellies help them hold onto the ground.
pages.brief: An earthworm stretches its body forward across damp soil, then pulls the rest of itself along. Its belly touches the ground, where tiny, tough hairs grip the surface. The worm is shown close-up, with its body long and thin as it moves.

pages.text: Slimy Worms! Earthworms’ bodies are covered in slime. The slime helps keep earthworms cool and wet. It also helps earthworms slide through soil.
pages.brief: An earthworm glistens with slime as it slides through dark, moist soil. Its wet body bends around small stones and dirt clumps, leaving a shiny trail. The slime keeps the worm cool and wet while it moves.

pages.text: After worms mate, a small ball of slime forms. The slime dries into a cocoon where baby worms can grow. Later, baby worms come out of the cocoon. How do earthworms breathe? Earthworms don’t breathe through their mouths. Instead, they breathe through their skin. That’s why you’ll often see earthworms on sidewalks when it rains. They can drown if they stay underground. Earthworms can’t survive if their skin dries out, either. They can only breathe when their skin is wet.
pages.brief: Two earthworms lie close together in moist soil, and a small slime ball forms nearby, drying into a cocoon. Later, tiny baby worms come out. On a wet sidewalk in the rain, an earthworm lies with shiny, wet skin so it can breathe.

pages.text: Earthworm Behavior Earthworms build long tunnels underground. The tunnels protect worms from heat and sunlight and they also help earthworms hide from hungry animals.
pages.brief: An earthworm tunnels through underground soil, leaving a long, open tunnel behind it. The tunnel curves through the dirt, giving the worm a sheltered path away from heat and sunlight. The worm stays deep in the soil, hidden from hungry animals above.

pages.text: Earthworms are sometimes called night crawlers because they come out at night to feed. They use their mouths to pull dead leaves and plants into their tunnels.
pages.brief: At night, an earthworm comes out of its tunnel onto dark soil. It grips a dead leaf with its mouth and pulls it down into the tunnel. Around it are fallen plant pieces on the ground, and the scene is dim.

pages.text: Earthworms Are Good for the Soil Farmers love earthworms! When earthworms dig tunnels, they create space in the soil. The space helps plants get the water and air they require to grow.
pages.brief: A farmer looks over rich garden soil where earthworms have tunneled. Small openings in the soil show spaces that let water and air reach plant roots. Young plants grow nearby, and the farmer watches the healthy ground.

pages.text: Some people raise earthworms on worm farms. The earthworms eat food scraps, turning them into rich soil. Earthworm waste helps plants grow big and healthy.
pages.brief: On a worm farm, food scraps lie in dark soil. Earthworms gather around the scraps and break them down, turning them into rich soil. Nearby, a plant grows big and healthy in the dark, crumbly soil.

pages.text: A mole (top left), a toad (bottom left), and a shrew (right) all make meals of worms. Wanted: Earthworms! Farmers aren’t the only ones who love earthworms. Moles, rats, and toads love juicy night crawlers. They love to eat them! Worms make good fishing bait because fish think earthworms are tasty, too. Earthworms are important food for these and other animals.
pages.brief: A mole, a toad, and a shrew are shown around a moist patch of soil, each looking toward an earthworm. A rat watches nearby, and a fish underwater eyes an earthworm used as fishing bait. The animals are grouped as worm eaters.

pages.text: An earthworm pokes its head out of its hole. Earthworms may be small, but they have a big job. Earthworms help plants grow!
pages.brief: An earthworm pokes its head out of a hole in the ground, its body partly hidden in the soil. Around the hole, small plants grow in the garden. The worm is tiny beside the plants, yet the soil looks healthy where it has been working.

books.title: Taj Mahal
books.art_why: The book tells a 1600s Mughal story and construction, before photographs could show these events.

pages.text: The Taj Mahal Hundreds of years ago, the Mughal (MOO-guhl) family ruled parts of India. They were rich and powerful rulers. They built many beautiful buildings that still stand today. Of all the places the Mughal people built, the most famous is the Taj Mahal (TAJ muh-HAHL) in Agra, India.
pages.brief: Mughal rulers in rich robes stand before grand buildings they built in India, while the white Taj Mahal rises in Agra in the distance. The scene shows a powerful family and the famous monument that still stands today.

pages.text: The Taj Mahal is a memorial with beautiful buildings, walls, and gates. It also has peaceful gardens and lovely pools of water. Shah Jahan (SHAH jah-HAHN) was an important Mughal ruler. He built the Taj Mahal over three hundred years ago for his wife after she died. Her name was Mumtaz Mahal (moom- TAHZ muh-HAHL). Shah Jahan wanted to make a beautiful burial place for her. He wanted people to remember her for a long time. Across the Yamuna River to the east is the Moonlight Garden. Experts think this was one of Shah Jahan’s favorite spots to view his wife’s memorial.
pages.brief: Shah Jahan stands across the Yamuna River in the Moonlight Garden, looking toward the Taj Mahal memorial. The buildings, walls, gates, peaceful gardens and pools of water are shown, built as a beautiful burial place for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

pages.text: Map of the Taj Mahal riverfront terrace tower mausoleum assembly hall (jawab) mosque central pool water channel gardens Great Gate forecourt.
pages.brief: An overhead drawing shows the Taj Mahal riverfront terrace beside a river, with a tower, mausoleum, assembly hall, mosque, central pool, water channel, gardens, Great Gate and forecourt arranged in a formal layout. The plan places the mausoleum and mosque near the water, with the gardens and forecourt around them.

pages.text: The Great Gate People enter the Taj Mahal through the Great Gate. Visitors can see the main building through the door of the gate. The huge white building is where Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal are buried. Four tall, thin towers are around it.
pages.brief: Visitors enter the Taj Mahal through the Great Gate. Through the doorway they see the huge white main building, where Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal are buried, surrounded by four tall, thin towers. The gate doorway frames the white monument beyond.

pages.text: The Main Building Some of the Taj Mahal’s buildings are made of red sandstone. The main building and the towers around it are made of white stone called marble. The Taj Mahal buildings have many beautiful things, both inside and outside. Artists used thousands of colorful stones to make flowers, butterflies, and other pictures on the walls. Different kinds of shiny gems were used as well.
pages.brief: Artists use thousands of colorful stones to make flowers, butterflies and other pictures on the white marble walls of the main building, while some nearby buildings are made of red sandstone. Shiny gems decorate the beautiful buildings inside and outside.

pages.text: Visitors can go inside the main building, where Shah Jahan and his wife are buried. A coffin for Mumtaz Mahal is in the center of the room. Her husband’s coffin is beside hers. Both coffins are empty. They are only for people to view. The real burial places are in a room under the main floor.
pages.brief: Inside the main building, visitors look at two empty coffins in the center of the room. Mumtaz Mahal's coffin is in the center, and Shah Jahan's coffin is beside hers. The real burial places lie in a room under the main floor.

pages.text: A Love Story Shah Jahan met his wife-to-be when he was fifteen and she was fourteen. They were married five years later. He gave her the title Mumtaz Mahal, which means “Chosen One of the Palace.” She was his wife and also his close friend.
pages.brief: Young Shah Jahan, fifteen, meets his future wife, fourteen, in a palace setting. Five years later they marry, and he gives her the title Mumtaz Mahal, meaning Chosen One of the Palace. The scene shows the young couple and their wedding.

pages.text: When Mumtaz died, Shah Jahan was heartbroken. People said he was so sad that his beard turned white, and he cried so much, he needed glasses.
pages.brief: Shah Jahan sits grieving with a white beard and glasses, his face full of sadness after Mumtaz Mahal's death. He looks down, heartbroken, in a Mughal palace room. People said his sorrow was so great that his beard turned white and he cried so much he needed glasses.

pages.text: The Buildings Go Up After Mumtaz Mahal died, Shah Jahan returned to his capital city of Agra, India. He decided to build the Taj Mahal in Agra beside the Yamuna (YAH-moo-nah) River. Shah Jahan began building the Taj Mahal in 1632, about a year after Mumtaz Mahal died.
pages.brief: After Mumtaz Mahal's death, Shah Jahan returns to Agra, India, beside the Yamuna River. He stands near the riverbank and decides to begin building the Taj Mahal there in 1632, about a year after her death.

pages.text: It was a big job. Twenty thousand workers helped build the Taj Mahal. One thousand elephants helped carry things. Builders and painters came from all over the world. Huge pieces of white marble were pulled on carts by oxen. Workers used ropes to move the marble into place. The work was finished in 1653.
pages.brief: At the construction site, twenty thousand workers and one thousand elephants help build the Taj Mahal. Builders and painters come from all over the world. Oxen pull carts carrying huge white marble pieces, and workers use ropes to move the marble into place. The work is finished in 1653.

pages.text: The Taj Mahal Today After Shah Jahan died, the Taj Mahal was forgotten. People stole many of the gems and stones from its walls. They also took gold lamps, beautiful rugs, and other things. Since then, people have fixed some of the damage at the Taj Mahal. Today, air pollution is the biggest danger. Pollution from factories damages the buildings and ruins the white marble. People work to keep the Taj Mahal safe. They moved some factories farther away. Groups of people work to fix harm caused by air pollution.
pages.brief: Today, workers clean and repair the white marble of the Taj Mahal as pollution haze drifts around it. Some factories stand farther away, and groups work to undo damage caused by air pollution to the buildings and marble.

pages.text: A Lasting Memorial Shah Jahan wanted to make a place for people to enjoy forever. Today, the Taj Mahal is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Many people visit every day to view the beautiful buildings and gardens. Hundreds of years have passed since the Taj Mahal was built. It is still one of the most beautiful places in the world.
pages.brief: Many visitors walk through the gardens toward the white Taj Mahal buildings, enjoying the lasting memorial Shah Jahan wanted people to enjoy forever. The scene shows the famous place today, one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

books.title: Real-Life Multiplication
books.art_why: The book shows real classroom and household objects that can be photographed.

pages.text: You and your friends are making an art project for a school art show. You are in charge of bringing buttons for the project. You empty the button box onto the table. There are so many buttons! Could there be twenty buttons? Fifty? How can you figure it out? Sometimes you need to find out how many objects are in a large group. Counting them is one way. But counting this many objects is tricky! When you count, you have to be sure that • you keep track of the buttons you have counted already • you don’t count any of the buttons twice • you don’t miss any buttons Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: A child empties a button box onto a table for a school art project, with many buttons spread out in a large pile; friends work nearby on the project.

pages.text: One way to make objects easier to count is to group them. Once the objects are in groups, you can add the number in each group to find the total. There are four dimes in one hand. There are six dimes in the other hand. You can add the number of dimes in each group to find the total. There are ten dimes in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Two open hands hold dimes, with four dimes in one hand and six dimes in the other; the dimes are grouped by hand so the total of ten dimes can be counted.

pages.text: There are three groups of baseball bats in the picture. There are two groups of four bats. There is one group of one bat. You can add the number of bats in each group to find the total. There are nine bats in all.
pages.brief: Baseball bats lie in three separate groups: two groups of four bats and one single bat, making nine bats in all.

pages.text: There is one ring on each finger of one hand. There are five rings in the first group. There is one ring on each finger of the other hand. There are five rings in the second group. There are two rings in the group on the table. You can add the number of rings in each group to find the total. There are twelve rings in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Two hands each wear one ring on every finger, showing five rings per hand, while two more rings sit in a small group on the table; together there are twelve rings.

pages.text: There are two groups with ten cubes in each group. In the third group, there is one cube. You can add the number of cubes in each group to find the total. There are twenty-one cubes in all.
pages.brief: Cubes are arranged in three groups: two groups with ten cubes each and a third group with one cube, making twenty-one cubes in all.

pages.text: There are three groups with two feet in each group. You can add the number of feet to find the total. There are six feet in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Three separate pairs of feet are shown as three groups, with two feet in each group, making six feet in all.

pages.text: There is another way to find a total. You can skip-count if there is the same number of objects in each group. There are three groups of two feet. There is the same number in each group. So, you can skip-count to find the total. There are six feet in all.
pages.brief: Three groups of two feet are shown with the same number in each group, arranged so the equal groups can be counted together to reach six feet.

pages.text: Each butterfly has two antennae. There are six butterflies. You can add the number of antennae to find the total. There are twelve antennae in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Six butterflies are shown with their antennae, each butterfly having two antennae, so the twelve antennae can be counted by adding the pairs.

pages.text: There are six groups of two antennae. There is the same number in each group. So, you can also skip-count to find the total. There are twelve antennae in all.
pages.brief: The antennae from six butterflies are shown as six equal groups of two, making it easy to count the twelve antennae by equal groups.

pages.text: There are three groups of toy cars. There are three cars in each group. You can add to find the total. There are nine toy cars in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Three groups of toy cars are lined up, with three cars in each group, making nine toy cars in all.

pages.text: Each group has the same number of cars. So, you can also skip-count to find the total. There are nine toy cars in all.
pages.brief: The same toy cars appear in three equal groups, each group holding three cars, so the nine cars can be counted by equal groups.

pages.text: There are five hands. Each hand has five fingers. You can add to find the total number of fingers. There are twenty-five fingers in all. Each group has the same number. So, you can also skip-count to find the total. There are twenty-five fingers in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Five open hands are shown with five fingers on each hand, giving twenty-five fingers in all; each hand forms an equal group of five.

pages.text: There are five bugs in this picture. Each bug has six legs. You can add to find the total number of legs. There are thirty legs in all. Each bug has the same number of legs. So, you can also skip-count to find the total. You can solve this problem another way. You can multiply. There are thirty legs in all. You read it like this: five times six equals thirty. The number sentence means that you have five groups of six items, and the total is thirty. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Five bugs are shown, each with six legs, and the thirty legs are visible across the bugs; the bugs form equal groups of six legs.

pages.text: There are thirty legs in all.
pages.brief: Thirty legs are shown together as a complete total, arranged so the full group can be seen at once; the legs are grouped for counting.

pages.text: There are ten cars in this train. There are ten bears in each car. You can add to find the total number of bears. There are one hundred bears in all. You can also skip-count to find the total. You can solve this problem another way. You can multiply. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: A train with ten cars is filled with bears, and each car holds ten bears, making ten equal groups of ten and one hundred bears in all.

pages.text: You read it like this: ten times ten equals one hundred. The number sentence means that you have ten groups of ten items, and the total is one hundred. There are one hundred bears in all. 100 one hundred.
pages.brief: One hundred bears are shown in ten equal groups of ten, making the total of one hundred bears clear; the bears are arranged so the ten groups can be counted together.

pages.text: There are four pizzas. Each pizza is cut into six pieces. You can add to find the total number of pieces. There are twenty-four pieces in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Four pizzas are shown, and each pizza is cut into six pieces, making twenty-four pieces in all; the pieces are grouped by pizza.

pages.text: You can also skip-count to find the total. There are twenty-four pieces of pizza in all.
pages.brief: The twenty-four pizza pieces are shown arranged for counting, with four pizzas each divided into six pieces so the total can be counted by equal groups.

pages.text: Which container has more objects? You can skip-count to find the total. Think of the container as an array. An array shows objects in rows and columns. There are two rows. There are six eggs in each row. You can write a multiplication sentence to find the total number of eggs. There are four rows. There are three limes in each row. You can write a multiplication sentence to find the total number of limes. 4 x 3 = 12 Both containers hold twelve objects. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Two containers are shown: one holds eggs in two rows of six, and the other holds limes in four rows of three; both containers hold twelve objects, shown as rows and columns.

pages.text: There are six ways you can arrange twelve in arrays. Here are all the other ways you can arrange twelve in arrays.
pages.brief: Six different arrays of twelve are shown, each arranged in rows and columns with a different pattern, so the same total of twelve appears in six separate rectangular arrangements.

pages.text: What number sentences could you write about these arrays? Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Several arrays of objects are shown in rows and columns, each with equal rows and an equal number in each row, ready for finding totals from the arrangements.

books.title: Karate
books.art_why: Karate is a real activity with real students, dojos, uniforms and belts, so photographs fit.

pages.text: What Is Karate? Karate is a martial art in which people don’t use weapons. The word karate means “empty hand” in Japanese.
pages.brief: A karate student stands in a dojo and practices an open-hand strike without any weapon. The student’s hands are empty as they move through a martial arts pose, with a calm, focused face and no equipment nearby.

pages.text: Many people believe that karate began in the 1600s on Okinawa (oh-kee-NAH-wah), an island between China and Japan. The people who lived on the island could not have weapons. They came up with karate as a way to defend themselves. Now, karate is popular all around the world.
pages.brief: Long ago on Okinawa, an island between China and Japan, people practice empty-hand defense because they cannot have weapons. Today, karate students of many ages train in dojos around the world, carrying the martial art far beyond the island.

pages.text: The Gym Karate students train at a dojo, or gym. When they enter a dojo, they bow their heads to show good manners. The karate teacher is called a sensei. The sensei has many lessons to pass on. Students learn to listen to their sensei and follow the rules of the dojo.
pages.brief: At the entrance of a dojo, karate students bow their heads to show good manners. Inside, a sensei stands before the class and passes on lessons, while students listen carefully and follow the rules of the gym.

pages.text: Belts Students have to wear the right clothes before they start to train. In the dojo, they wear a special robe, or gi, with a colored belt around the waist. Students move on to different colored belts as they train and gain new skills. However, getting a new belt isn’t just about learning new moves.
pages.brief: In the dojo, karate students wear a special robe called a gi, tied with a colored belt around the waist. One student stands ready in the uniform, and different colored belts hang nearby as students move on to new skills.

pages.text: While students earn belts, they learn many good habits, such as self-control and patience. They can use these skills in other areas of their lives. The good habits students learn are just as important as the moves they practice.
pages.brief: Karate students practice self-control and patience in the dojo. One student waits calmly with focused hands while another practices a move, and both show good habits that they can use in other areas of their lives.

pages.text: Students earn new colored belts in a certain order. One story tells the meaning of each color through the growth of a plant. The different colors of the belts stand for the colors of the plant, the Sun, and the sky. A student grows much like a young plant. They grow as time passes and gain more skills.
pages.brief: A young plant grows beside a karate student, with colored belts arranged in order. The belt colors stand for the plant, the Sun, and the sky, and the student grows in skill as time passes, much like the young plant.

pages.text: Learning Karate Students learn karate in three main steps: kihon, kata, and kumite.
pages.brief: A karate class gathers in the dojo, with students split into three practice groups. One group works on basic moves, one practices a routine, and one practices with partners, as the students learn the three main steps of karate.

pages.text: Kihon Kihon is the set of moves for beginners. In kihon, students learn to breathe correctly and stand in the right position. They also learn how to do kicks, punches, blocks, and other moves. It is important for them to learn patience. Students practice until they are perfect.
pages.brief: In the dojo, beginner karate students stand in the right position and breathe correctly. They practice kicks, punches, blocks, and other moves again and again, working with patience and focused faces until their movements become perfect.

pages.text: Kata Kata is putting the moves from kihon into a routine. Students pretend to fight off attackers and learn to defend themselves. They also practice their flow from one move to the next. There are many different katas to learn.
pages.brief: Students practice kata by putting the moves from kihon into a routine. They pretend to fight off attackers and defend themselves, moving smoothly from one move to the next as they practice many different katas in the dojo.

pages.text: Many students also practice bunkai while learning kata. In bunkai, students learn why the moves from kata are useful. They learn to slow down and think about each move before they do it.
pages.brief: While learning kata in the dojo, students also practice bunkai. They slow down and think carefully about each move before they do it, exploring why the moves from kata are useful and how each one works for defense.

pages.text: Kumite After a lot of hard work, karate students reach the last step. In kumite, they use everything they have learned by practicing moves on one another.
pages.brief: After much hard work, karate students reach the last step, kumite. Two students face each other in the dojo and practice moves on one another with focused care, using everything they have learned in their training.

pages.text: Conclusion For many years, people around the world have learned good habits through karate. They have also worked hard to become stronger and faster, and to earn new belts. Some students hope to become karate masters, and everyone has a lot of fun trying to get there.
pages.brief: Karate students of many ages train together in the dojo, working hard to become stronger and faster and to earn new belts. Some students hope to become karate masters, and everyone has fun trying to get there.

books.title: The Butterfly Life Cycle
books.art_why: Monarch butterflies and their life stages exist in the real world today, so photographs are appropriate.

pages.text: The Butterfly Life Cycle.
pages.brief: A butterfly with wide patterned wings rests on a leaf in a garden, shown alone against soft green plants. The butterfly is the main subject, with its wings open so the patterns are clear and easy to see.

pages.text: The Life Cycle A monarch butterfly has four stages in its life cycle. They are egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult.
pages.brief: Four clear stages of a monarch butterfly are shown in order: a tiny oval egg on a leaf, a striped caterpillar, a green pupa hanging from a branch, and an adult monarch with orange and black wings. Each stage is separate and easy to see.

pages.text: Egg A female monarch butterfly lays an egg on the bottom of a leaf. She might lay several hundred eggs in her lifetime. The eggs are oval shaped. A caterpillar grows inside the tiny egg. The egg hatches in three to twelve days.
pages.brief: A female monarch butterfly clings to the underside of a green leaf, bending her body to lay a tiny oval egg. The egg is shown close up on the leaf's bottom surface, with a small caterpillar shape visible inside it.

pages.text: The hungry caterpillar eats all the time. It needs a lot of food to grow. First, the caterpillar eats its own eggshell. Then, the caterpillar eats the leaf it is on.
pages.brief: A striped monarch caterpillar sits on a green leaf, chewing the leaf edge. Beside it, a broken eggshell shows where it hatched. The caterpillar is surrounded by green leaves, with its mouth close to the leaf as it eats.

pages.text: The caterpillar grows quickly, but its skin does not grow. The caterpillar’s old skin splits and peels away. The caterpillar will shed the old skin many times in this stage.
pages.brief: A growing monarch caterpillar is shown beside its old skin, which has split and is peeling away from its body. The caterpillar looks larger and stretched, with the old skin behind it on a leaf, ready to be shed.

pages.text: Do You Know? Monarch caterpillars only eat the leaves of the milkweed plant. New skin is under the old skin. It is soft at first but soon hardens. The caterpillar sheds its skin four to six times and eats the old skin each time. The caterpillar grows for two to four weeks.
pages.brief: A monarch caterpillar clings to a milkweed leaf and eats the leaf edge. Its old skin has split open, showing soft new skin underneath. Beside it, a small piece of old skin rests on the leaf after being shed, and the caterpillar looks larger than before.

pages.text: Pupa When the caterpillar is grown, it hangs from a branch to prepare for the next stage. It sheds its skin one last time. The new skin is bright green and looks like a leaf.
pages.brief: A full-grown monarch caterpillar hangs upside down from a thin branch. Its old skin is slipping away for the last time, revealing bright green new skin underneath. The green covering is shaped like a small leaf and clings close to the caterpillar's body.

pages.text: This green skin hardens around the caterpillar. It will protect it from other animals as it changes inside. The caterpillar becomes a pupa. It will stay inside its shell for one to two weeks. During this time, big changes happen to its body.
pages.brief: A bright green pupa hangs from a branch, its hard shell smooth around the changing caterpillar inside. The pupa is shown close up against green leaves, protected from other animals while big changes happen inside its shell over time.

pages.text: Adult Butterfly An adult butterfly comes out of the shell. Its wet wings are folded against its body.
pages.brief: An adult monarch butterfly pushes out of the split pupa shell. Its wet wings are folded tightly against its body, and the empty green shell hangs behind it on a branch. The butterfly looks soft and newly emerged.

pages.text: The new butterfly rests. The butterfly must hang upside down, or it will not be able to fly. Blood pumping into the wings causes them to unfold and spread out.
pages.brief: A newly emerged monarch butterfly hangs upside down from a branch, resting. Its wings are still folded and wet. Blood pumps into the wings, making them begin to unfold and spread out from the butterfly's body.

pages.text: The butterfly hangs for several hours. The sun and air dry its delicate wings. A butterfly has two pairs of wings. They are covered in scales. The wings in the front often have a different pattern from the pair in the back. The colors on the wings are usually similar to each other.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly hangs upside down in warm sunlight, its delicate wings drying in the air. The two pairs of wings are covered in tiny scales. The front wings show a different pattern from the back pair, while their colors are similar to each other.

pages.text: Once the butterfly is able to fly, it flies off to eat. Unlike a caterpillar, a butterfly does not eat leaves. Instead, it sips sweet liquid from flowers. It also searches for a mate.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly flies from a branch toward a flower, ready to eat. It sips sweet liquid from the flower instead of eating leaves. Nearby, another monarch butterfly is shown as it searches for a mate in the garden.

pages.text: Adult butterflies do not grow. They save their energy for flying and laying eggs. Females are bigger than males. A monarch butterfly may only live for two to six weeks. After she finds a mate, the female monarch lays her eggs. The butterfly life cycle starts all over again.
pages.brief: An adult female monarch butterfly rests on a leaf, larger than a nearby male. She saves energy for flying and laying eggs, then lays eggs on a leaf. The eggs show that the butterfly life cycle will start all over again.

books.title: Stonehenge
books.art_why: Stonehenge was built thousands of years ago, so its building and ancient life can only be shown in drawings.

pages.text: An Ancient Monument There is an ancient monument in England that is made of dirt and giant stones. It is called Stonehenge, and it was built thousands of years ago. Scientists called archaeologists have been studying it for a long time. They are trying to learn how and why it was built. They also want to know more about the people who built it.
pages.brief: A wide drawing of Stonehenge standing on open English ground, ring of giant upright stones with lintels on top, circled by a low ditch and raised mound of dirt. Two archaeologists kneel at the base of a stone, brushing soil away, notebooks and small tools beside them.

pages.text: Earth and Giant Stones From the sky, Stonehenge looks like a small circle inside a big circle. The bigger circle is a ditch around a raised mound of dirt. The giant stones in the outer circle are made of a type of sandstone. Stones called lintels once lay atop the giant stones to connect them all together. The inner stones are made of three parts, and they form a horseshoe shape. Two stones stand upright, and one lintel lies across them. Other rocks in the circle are made of bluestone. An artist shows how Stonehenge might have looked before any stones fell over.
pages.brief: A view from high in the sky showing Stonehenge as a small circle inside a big circle: an outer ditch around a raised dirt mound, tall sandstone sarsen stones joined by lintels, and an inner horseshoe of paired uprights with a lintel across, plus smaller bluestones.

pages.text: Stonehenge lintel sarsen stone • The whole monument of Stonehenge is about the length of a football field. • Today, seventeen upright giant stones make up the outer circle. Experts think there used to be thirty. • The giant stones are very tall and heavy. Some of them weigh more than a school bus! trilithon bluestones.
pages.brief: A close study view of the stones: a tall upright sarsen with a lintel resting across two uprights forming a trilithon, smaller bluestones beside them, and a school bus drawn next to one giant stone to show its height and weight.

pages.text: Where Is Stonehenge? Stonehenge sits in an open field in southern England. Experts say people have been living in that area for about ten thousand years. The settlement may have been one of the biggest in England at one time. Long ago, the area was covered in trees. People cut them down to clear land for farming.
pages.brief: An open field in southern England with Stonehenge in the distance. In front, people with simple stone tools clear trees, stumps and fallen trunks lying about, opening farmland where a woodland once stood.

pages.text: Building Stonehenge Experts believe that people started building Stonehenge about five thousand years ago. Back then, people only had simple stone tools, not powerful machines. They did almost everything with their minds and muscles. The stones must have been brought to Stonehenge from far away. Tests have been done to prove it was possible to move the stones to Stonehenge. Stones were put on wooden sleds and dragged on wooden rails greased with animal fat.
pages.brief: Builders thousands of years ago haul a huge stone on a wooden sled along greased wooden rails, ropes over their shoulders, animal fat in a pot nearby. Other workers hold simple stone tools and stand watching in an open landscape.

pages.text: Lifting the standing stones must have been very hard. Experts think the builders might have dug holes and then tipped the bottoms of the stones into the holes. Then they could be pulled upright using ropes. Workers might have slid the tops of the arches up ramps built of dirt and wood. Then the tops could be set on the standing stones. No one knows for sure how the builders built Stonehenge. They did not leave pictures or writing to explain how they did it. That is why Stonehenge is still a big mystery.
pages.brief: Builders raise a standing stone: a hole dug in the ground, the stone's base tipped in, workers pulling ropes to haul it upright. Beside them a long ramp of dirt and wood leads up toward the top of two standing stones.

pages.text: An Outdoor Temple Why was Stonehenge built? Archaeologists continue to look and dig for clues about its purpose. One clue is that it was built away from where most people lived. Experts think Stonehenge was a temple of some kind. People probably came there for special events. They might have visited to remember dead relatives.
pages.brief: Stonehenge stands alone as an outdoor temple, away from any settlement. A group of people gathers inside the stone circle for a special event, standing quietly together to remember relatives who have died.

pages.text: Stonehenge was also a graveyard. Archaeologists have found the bodies of about 240 people nearby.
pages.brief: Archaeologists work in a shallow grave near Stonehenge, carefully uncovering buried human remains in the earth, with bones laid out and small tools and brushes set beside the open ground.

pages.text: Another idea about Stonehenge is that it lines up with the sun’s movements. The sun shines through certain parts of the monument when the seasons change. This was important information for farmers long ago. It helped them figure out the best time to plant their crops.
pages.brief: Low sunlight shines through a gap between the standing stones of Stonehenge at the change of season. Beyond the monument, farmers in a field bend to plant crops, watching the sun's position.

pages.text: Stonehenge Today More than nine hundred thousand people visit Stonehenge each year. The visitor center has stone tools and other ancient objects. There are huts to show what life was like long ago. Volunteers show visitors ancient skills such as pottery and rope making.
pages.brief: Visitors walk around Stonehenge today. Nearby, a visitor centre shows stone tools and ancient objects on display, round huts stand to show old life, and a volunteer sits shaping pottery while another twists rope.

pages.text: Archaeologists continue to explore the Stonehenge site. They use new tools such as radar that can find objects underground. This helps them make more discoveries faster.
pages.brief: Archaeologists survey the Stonehenge site, one pushing a radar device on a wheeled frame across the grass while another watches a screen, searching for objects buried underground beneath the standing stones.

pages.text: Ancient Wonder No one knows for sure why ancient people built Stonehenge. How they did it is also a mystery. Still, Stonehenge continues to fill people with wonder thousands of years after it was built.
pages.brief: Stonehenge at golden evening light, the great circle of upright stones and lintels standing on the open plain, a few visitors small beside them, gazing up in wonder at the ancient monument.

books.title: Canada
books.art_why: Landform and wildlife scenes are shown as illustrated views of Canada's regions.

pages.text: Where Is It? Canada is the biggest country in North America. It is so big that it reaches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. Canada is farther north than most other countries.
pages.brief: A vast northern land stretches from one great ocean on the left to another ocean on the right, with cold blue water at both edges and wide green and grey land between. Thin ice and snow hint at the far north, showing how far the country reaches upward toward the pole.

pages.text: Canada has only one neighbor, the United States. Ottawa is the country’s capital. The city’s buildings are fun to visit.
pages.brief: A single long borderline runs along the bottom of a wide country, with one neighbouring country below it. Above the line, the capital city rises with stone government buildings, towers and walkways, and visitors stroll between them looking up at the facades.

pages.text: People Nearly all Canadians speak French, English, or both. Canada’s Indigenous peoples include more than 600 groups of First Nations. They also include the Inuit and Métis. People come from faraway countries to live in Canada.
pages.brief: Many different people stand together in a bright street: First Nations, Inuit and Métis people in traditional clothing beside newcomers from faraway countries. Two people chat, one speaking French and one speaking English, and children listen beside them.

pages.text: Together, all of these different people make Canada strong. Most Canadians live in big cities in the south of Canada. Few people live in the far north.
pages.brief: A crowd of many different faces stands shoulder to shoulder, smiling, showing how the country's strength comes from its mix of people. Behind them, tall city towers fill the southern skyline, while far in the distance a snowy, empty northern plain stretches away with almost nobody on it.

pages.text: Land Canada has many different landforms. In the west are rows of steep mountains. Then there are flat or rolling plains. A high, flat area with thousands of lakes is in the middle.
pages.brief: A wide landscape shows rows of steep rocky mountains in the west, then flat and gently rolling grassland plains, then a high flat plateau in the middle dotted with thousands of small blue lakes shining between the rocks and moss.

pages.text: The land in the south is where most of the cities are. In the east are hills. In the north, the land is covered with ice and snow.
pages.brief: A long view moves from green southern land full of city buildings and streets, across soft eastern hills, up to the far north where the ground is buried under thick ice and snow under a pale sky.

pages.text: Animals Some animals live only in the cold north. Others live only in the mountains or forests. Polar bears and harp seals live in the north. They both have white fur to hide on the snow.
pages.brief: On the northern snow, a polar bear walks across the ice while a harp seal lies nearby on the white surface. Both animals have thick white fur that blends into the snowy ground around them.

pages.text: Big sheep and goats live in the mountains. They have feet that help them climb rocks. Many animals in Canada move in winter and spring. Canada geese fly south every winter. They return in the spring when it is warmer.
pages.brief: Big sheep and goats with sure, gripping feet pick their way up a rocky mountain slope. Above them, a long line of Canada geese flies in a V shape, heading south over forests and open water.

pages.text: Celebrations All across Canada, people celebrate winter. There are festivals for ice-skating and ice carving. There are dogsled races across the snow.
pages.brief: A winter festival fills a snowy town: skaters glide on a frozen rink, a carver shapes a block of ice with tools, and a team of dogs pulls a sled racing across the snow while people cheer from the side.

pages.text: The biggest winter festival is in Quebec City. There is an ice castle to visit and games to play.
pages.brief: In Quebec City, a shining castle built entirely of ice stands in a snowy square. Children and grown-ups play games around it, climbing and laughing in thick coats, scarves and mittens.

pages.text: Conclusion Canada is a very big country with many different landforms and animals. It has many different people, too. Canadians say their differences make them strong.
pages.brief: A grand spread of the whole country: mountains, plains, lakes, forests and icy northern ground, with polar bears, geese and mountain goats, and many different people standing together in front of the varied landscape.

pages.text: Canada Population: 38,000,000 Land: 9,984,670 square kilometers (3,855,103 sq. mi.) Capital City: Ottawa Official Languages: English and French Currency: Canadian dollar.
pages.brief: A busy street in the capital city shows many people of different backgrounds talking together in English and French, with tall government buildings behind them, and Canadian dollar coins and notes held in people's hands.

books.title: Rainbows
books.art_why: The book explains light with diagram-like scenes and a historical scientist, best shown as drawing.

pages.text: Introduction When the Sun comes out after it rains, run outside. You may see a rainbow in the sky.
pages.brief: After rain, the Sun breaks through clouds. A person runs outside into open air, looking up at the sky. A rainbow arcs across the sky above. Wet ground and bright sunlight show the moment just after a rain shower.

pages.text: Rainbows are tricks made by light. We can see them, but we can’t touch them or walk around them. They seem to move away when we try to get close to them. Science can explain how rainbows happen.
pages.brief: A rainbow glows in the distance above a landscape. A person reaches toward it but cannot touch it. The rainbow seems to shift farther away as the person steps closer. Soft sunlight and light rain fill the air, showing the rainbow as a trick of light.

pages.text: Where and When Rainbows Appear Look around the next time you see a rainbow. The Sun will be shining from behind you. There will be rain in front of you, where you’ll see the rainbow.
pages.brief: A person stands outdoors with the Sun shining from behind them. In front of them, rain falls and a rainbow appears in the rain. The person looks toward the rainbow, with bright sunlight at their back and wet air ahead.

pages.text: Rainbows need water drops and sunlight to form. They can even form under a bright moon. These are called moonbows.
pages.brief: Water drops and sunlight fill the air as a rainbow forms. In another scene, a bright moon shines over falling water drops and a faint moonbow appears in the night sky. The air is moist, and light passes through the drops.

pages.text: We usually see a rainbow as a half circle. It actually forms a full circle. From the ground, we can only see the top half.
pages.brief: A rainbow arcs across the sky as a half circle seen from the ground. Above, a fuller circular rainbow surrounds an unseen center, showing the full circle. A person on the ground looks up at only the top half.

pages.text: How Rainbows Form Years ago, a French scientist studied rainbows. He found that to see a rainbow, you must be in the right spot. Rainbows in Myths and Tales.
pages.brief: A French scientist from long ago studies rainbows outdoors, watching light and water in the sky. He stands in the right spot to see the rainbow. Around him, the scene suggests old stories and myths about rainbows.

pages.text: Knowing how light moves helps explain rainbows. Think of running on land. Now think of trying to run through water. You will move more slowly through water because it is thicker than air. In the same way, light moves faster through air than through water. As the light moves through water, it slows down and bends.
pages.brief: A runner moves quickly on dry land and more slowly through water. Beside this, a beam of light travels through air and then enters water, where it slows and bends. The two scenes show how moving through water is slower and thicker than air.

pages.text: Light bends as it enters the drop. The sunlight splits into many colors. 2 Light reflects from the back of the drop. 3 Light bends again as it leaves the drop. Rainbows form when water drops meet sunlight. The light bends when it goes into each drop. Then it reflects, or bounces, off the back of each drop. The light bends again as it leaves the drop. This happens in millions of water drops at once, making the colors of a rainbow.
pages.brief: A close view of a water drop shows sunlight entering and bending. The light splits into many colors, reflects from the back of the drop, and bends again as it leaves. Millions of water drops do this together, making the colors of a rainbow.

pages.text: The Colors of the Rainbow Sunlight is made up of many colors. Water drops split the sunlight into different colors. Splitting light makes a rainbow. You have to be in the right spot to see a rainbow. Each water drop reflects colored light at a slightly different angle.
pages.brief: Sunlight enters water drops and splits into many colors. Each drop reflects colored light at a slightly different angle. A person stands in the right spot to see the rainbow made by countless drops splitting light across the sky.

pages.text: The colors of the rainbow always appear in the same order. The name ROY G. BIV can help you remember the seven main colors. They are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Make Your Own Rainbow 1. Fill a clear glass about three-quarters full of water. 2. Place the glass where sunlight can pass through it. 3. Hold a white piece of paper. Let the light shine through the water onto the paper. Move the paper around until you find a rainbow. 4. Use colored pencils to mark the different colors on the paper. How many can you see? What order are they in?
pages.brief: A clear glass three-quarters full of water sits in sunlight. A white paper catches light shining through the water, and a rainbow appears on the paper. Colored pencils mark the colors in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

pages.text: Conclusion Rain stops and the Sun comes out. A beautiful rainbow sweeps across the sky. Most people find it hard not to stop and stare when a rainbow appears.
pages.brief: Rain stops and the Sun comes out. A beautiful rainbow sweeps across the sky above a landscape. People outdoors stop and stare up at the bright arc, unable to look away from the colorful sight.

pages.text: Science explains how rainbows form. Still, a rainbow is always a magical sight to see.
pages.brief: A rainbow shines across the sky as sunlight passes through water drops. The scene shows the scientific cause of the rainbow, yet the sight remains magical and beautiful. A person gazes at it, taking in the colorful arc.

books.title: Petra
books.art_why: Petra’s people and construction are from more than two thousand years ago, before photographs existed.

pages.text: Rock City More than two thousand years ago, a group of people built an amazing city in the Middle East. They used special tools to carve buildings out of mountains. These people were the Nabataeans (nab-uh-TEE-uns). Their beautiful rock city was Petra.
pages.brief: A group of Nabataean builders use special tools to carve tall buildings out of a mountain in the Middle Eastern desert more than two thousand years ago; the beautiful rock city of Petra rises from the cliffs around them.

pages.text: Petra SYRIA IRAQ Amman DEAD SEA ISRAEL JORDAN Petra EUROPE ASIA EGYPT Ma’an AFRICA RED SEA SAUDI ARABIA City in the Desert Petra is in the country of Jordan, in one of Earth’s driest deserts. Red sandstone cliffs and canyons are all that can be seen for many miles. A canyon called the Siq (SEEK) leads to Petra. It is the main way to reach the city. the Siq.
pages.brief: Red sandstone cliffs and canyons stretch across the dry desert in Jordan; the narrow Siq canyon cuts between high rock walls as the main way to reach Petra, with the Dead Sea, Red Sea, and surrounding lands beyond.

pages.text: Buried City The city of Petra is 264 square kilometers (102 sq. mi.). The downtown area is 6 square kilometers (2 sq. mi.). The city has hundreds of tombs and other structures. Most of Petra is still buried under the ground. Scientists find more structures as they dig it up. Colonnaded Street.
pages.brief: Hundreds of tombs and other structures spread across Petra’s large desert site, while much of the buried city remains under the ground; scientists dig in the dust to uncover more structures, with the Colonnaded Street visible among the ruins.

pages.text: The Treasury is the first structure visitors see after they pass through the Siq. The Treasury is Petra’s best-known structure. The Royal Tombs are where they buried their kings. Other famous structures include the Theatre, Petra Museum, and the Monastery. Many structures are over 30 meters (100 ft.) tall. The Nabataeans also made many structures to collect, store, and carry water. They could not have lived in such a dry place without a way to get and hold water.
pages.brief: Visitors pass through the Siq and see the Treasury, Petra’s best-known structure, carved into the rock; nearby are the Royal Tombs where kings were buried, the Theatre, Petra Museum, and Monastery, while Nabataean structures collect and store water.

pages.text: A Journey Through Petra Entrance to the Siq Visitor Centre Path through the Siq Treasury Street of Facades Theatre Royal Tombs Colonnaded Street Monastery Petra Museum Walking east to west from the Visitor Centre to the Monastery takes about twenty minutes at a normal pace. Most visitors take much longer, though, as they stop to look at each new place.
pages.brief: Visitors walk east to west from the Visitor Centre, through the narrow Siq and past the Treasury, Street of Facades, Theatre, Royal Tombs, Colonnaded Street, Monastery, and Petra Museum; most stop often to look at each new place along the way.

pages.text: A Busy Trade Center Long ago, people from the Middle East, Asia, and Africa crossed the desert to trade with each other. They traveled through the land where the Nabataeans lived. The Nabataeans took care of camels, goats, and sheep. At first, they wandered from place to place. Later, they grew rich, settled down, and built Petra. Scientists think the Nabataeans built the Rose City around 300 bce. Over time, it became a busy trade center.
pages.brief: Traders from the Middle East, Asia, and Africa cross the desert with camels and goods, while Nabataeans tend camels, goats, and sheep nearby; the Nabataeans settle down and build Petra around 300 bce, and it becomes a busy trade center.

pages.text: Not much is known about the Nabataeans, but it is known that they worshipped the Sun. Scientists know this from studying Petra’s most important structures. On certain days of the year, the Sun lights up special parts of these structures. The Nabataeans must have built them on purpose so the Sun would shine on them that way.
pages.brief: Nabataean worshippers gather at a tall structure carved into the rock as the Sun shines on a special part of the stone; the sunlight falls there on a certain day of the year, showing that the Nabataeans built the structure on purpose.

pages.text: The Romans had a big empire based in Italy. Romans took over Petra in 106 ce. People’s lives mostly stayed the same. They built new structures that looked more like Roman structures. A huge earthquake in 363 ce broke Petra’s water system. People started leaving the city at that time. Another big earthquake happened in 551. Arabs took over Petra about a hundred years later. The last people left Petra soon after.
pages.brief: Roman officials stand among new Roman-style structures in Petra, while a broken water system and cracked stones show earthquake damage; families leave the city after the earthquakes, and later Arab newcomers arrive before the last people depart.

pages.text: Building Petra Many of Petra’s structures are carved right into the mountains. Others are built from sandstone taken from the mountains. A few structures use both methods. Scientists are certain that Petra’s carved structures were made from the top down. They know this because some structures were never finished. They are only carved at the top. No one knows for sure how the Nabataeans made the carved structures. Some scientists think they removed large blocks of sandstone, leaving huge rock steps. Carvers would have stood on the steps as they worked up high.
pages.brief: Nabataean carvers stand on huge rock steps high on a cliff, carving a structure from the top down; an unfinished facade nearby is carved only at the top, while other Petra structures are built from sandstone blocks taken from the mountains.

pages.text: Other scientists think the carvers put strong pins into the rock. Then they rested a wooden board on the pins. They would have stood on the board while they worked. Scientists hope to learn more as they keep studying Petra.
pages.brief: Nabataean carvers stand on a wooden board supported by strong pins set into the rock face, working high on a structure; the pins and board show one idea about how the Nabataeans carved Petra’s high rock buildings.

pages.text: Seeing Petra More than four hundred thousand people visit Petra each year. No cars are allowed, so many people walk through the Siq to get there. Others ride a horse, donkey, or camel. Visitors walk around Petra on their own. It can take up to five days to see everything!
pages.brief: Many visitors walk through the narrow Siq toward Petra, while others ride horses, donkeys, or camels; no cars are allowed, and visitors wander around the rock city on their own, with some taking up to five days to see everything.

pages.text: New Discoveries Scientists learn more about Petra all the time. Not long ago, they found pools, gardens, and fountains. Every discovery shows more about how smart the Nabataeans were. They figured out how to bring water to a very dry desert. Long ago, people came to Petra because of water. More than two thousand years later, they come to see a beautiful rock city.
pages.brief: Scientists uncover pools, gardens, and fountains among Petra’s stones, showing how the Nabataeans brought water to the dry desert; visitors look at the beautiful rock city that people once came to for water more than two thousand years later.

books.title: Slithery Snakes
books.art_why: Real snakes and their habitats exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Snakes are reptiles. There are several thousand kinds of snakes. They live in oceans, in trees, and on land, and they survive in unusual ways.
pages.brief: Several snakes are shown in the ocean, in a tree, and on land. One swims through water, one rests among branches, and one moves across the ground, illustrating where snakes live and how they survive in unusual ways.

pages.text: Wild snakes live almost everywhere on Earth except Antarctica and some islands. Some wild snakes may live as long as twenty-five years. Biggest and Smallest The largest snake is the green anaconda. A full-grown green anaconda can be close to 10 meters (33 ft.) long and weigh more than 230 kilograms (507 lb.). One of the smallest snakes is the thread snake. It is only about 12 centimeters (4 in.) long.
pages.brief: A huge green anaconda stretches through shallow water, its thick body nearly ten meters long and very heavy. Nearby, a tiny thread snake lies on the ground, only about twelve centimeters long, showing the biggest and smallest snakes.

pages.text: Snake Traits Snakes are cold-blooded. Their body temperature changes with the temperature around them. Snakes find sunshine to stay warm. They find shade to stay cool. During winter, some snakes stay underground or under rock piles to stay warm. Snakes also rest in groups to share body heat.
pages.brief: A snake lies in bright sunshine to warm its cold-blooded body. Another rests in cool shade. One is tucked underground near a rock pile for winter warmth, and two snakes rest together in a group to share body heat.

pages.text: Snakes have long backbones. Their backbones have many separate bones, which lets them move in many ways. A snake’s body is covered in scales. The scales protect it. They also help keep the snake dry. The scales grow from its skin. Snakes use their scales and muscles to move. The scales on their belly grab the surface beneath them. Their muscles help them move along the ground. Some snakes even use their muscles and scales to climb trees.
pages.brief: A snake moves over the ground, its belly scales gripping the surface as muscles bend its long body. Another snake climbs a tree trunk, using the same scales and muscles. A close view shows the separate scales covering its skin.

pages.text: Snake scales look like a single sheet of skin. Snakes don’t shed skin. Instead, they shed the outer layers of their scales up to four times per year. This is called molting. When molting, snakes rub against something like a rock or log. This helps their outer layer stretch and split. Young snakes shed more because they grow fast. Snakes also shed to get rid of pests on their scales.
pages.brief: A snake rubs its body against a rough rock, and the outer layer of its scales begins to stretch and split. A patch of old, shed skin lies nearby. This molting snake is replacing the outer layers of its scales.

pages.text: Snakes have clear scales instead of eyelids. The scales keep their eyes from drying out. Snakes cannot blink. Snakes do not have ears you can see. Instead, sound passes through their jaws to their inner ears, which sends the sound to their brain.
pages.brief: A close view of a snake's head shows clear scales over its eyes instead of eyelids, keeping the eyes from drying out. No ear openings are visible on the side of its head. The snake cannot blink.

pages.text: Another important feature of a snake is its tongue. Snakes use their tongue to smell. Smells in the air stick to their tongue. They identify the smell using special sacs behind their nose. Some snakes can sense the heat of animals nearby. Pits near the snake’s eyes sense heat. These snakes can tell how far away something is in the dark when they hunt.
pages.brief: A snake's head is shown with its tongue extended, picking up smells from the air. Small pits near its eyes are visible. The snake can sense the heat of animals nearby and tell how far away something is in the dark.

pages.text: Hunting and Eating Snakes are meat eaters. Some snakes inject venom when biting prey. Other snakes squeeze prey to death. Some snakes swallow prey alive. Most snakes’ jaws are loosely connected. This lets snakes open their mouth wide to swallow large prey. Snakes’ fangs and other teeth point backward, helping push food toward their throat. Snakes have a breathing tube that they push out of their mouth. This lets them breathe when they swallow prey. Muscles move it to the stomach. Stomach acids turn prey into liquid so the snake can digest it easier.
pages.brief: A snake opens its loosely connected jaws wide around a large prey animal, its backward-pointing teeth helping push the food toward its throat. Another snake coils tightly around prey, squeezing it. A third snake swallows prey alive.

pages.text: How Snakes Are Born Most female snakes that live in cold areas lay eggs in late spring or early summer. Snakes that live in warmer areas may mate at any time of year. Baby snakes may grow sharp teeth to cut through the eggs. Once they hatch, they must survive on their own and face many dangers. Some female snakes keep eggs inside their body until they hatch. Then they give birth to live babies.
pages.brief: A baby snake pushes out of an egg, sharp teeth at its mouth to cut through the shell. Nearby, another female snake gives birth to live young. The baby snakes are on their own and face many dangers.

pages.text: Venomous Snakes Venom is a dangerous liquid. Some snakes inject venom when they bite with their fangs. Venom is made in sacs behind the snake’s eyes. It flows through the snake’s fangs from these sacs.
pages.brief: A venomous snake is shown with its mouth open and long fangs exposed. A bead of venom appears at a fang tip. The area behind its eyes is visible, where venom is made in sacs before flowing through the fangs.

pages.text: Snakes use venom to defend and attack. Snakes usually inject more venom when biting in defense. The venom paralyzes their prey. Some snakes inject venom and let the prey go. Then they follow the prey until it dies. Other snakes use their teeth or body to hold on to prey until it dies. Then they eat it. Venom versus Poison Venom and poison are not the same thing. Poison is absorbed through the skin, eaten, or inhaled. Venom is injected into the victim through a bite or sting.
pages.brief: A snake strikes in defense, fangs exposed, injecting venom into a bite. Another snake follows weakened prey from a distance. A third snake holds prey with its body and teeth until the prey dies.

pages.text: Conclusion Snakes are amazing hunters. They have survived almost everywhere. Snakes are unusual animals that play an important role in our environment.
pages.brief: Several snakes appear in different places—one on land, one in a tree, and one near water. Each is alert, showing snakes as amazing hunters that have survived almost everywhere and play an important role in the environment.

books.title: Istanbul
books.art_why: Historical city scenes and long-ago events call for illustration rather than photography.

pages.text: One City, Two Worlds A ship sails into the port of a big city. It came from Europe and is on its way to Asia. This is Istanbul, Turkey. Parts of this amazing city are on each continent. Wowser! Istanbul is one of only a few cities in the world on two continents.
pages.brief: A ship sails into the port of a big city, arriving from Europe and heading toward Asia. This is Istanbul, Turkey. Parts of the amazing city lie on each continent, showing that Istanbul is one of only a few cities in the world on two continents.

pages.text: Where in the World? Istanbul is in the northwest corner of Turkey. It is on both sides of a narrow waterway between two seas. Istanbul has the most people of any city in Europe. A Bridge Between Continents EUROPE ASIA EUROPE Istanbul AFRICA BLACK SEA Istanbul SEA OF MARMARA ASIA Italy AEGEAN SEA Turkey MEDITERRANEAN SEA.
pages.brief: A wide view shows Istanbul in Turkey’s northwest corner, split by a narrow waterway between two seas. Land lies on both the European and Asian sides, with nearby seas and countries around the city. The city sits where two continents meet.

pages.text: History Istanbul has been an important port since long ago. It is on the only road between the two seas. People from both the East and West come to Istanbul for many reasons. Byzas (BY-zuhss) led people to the area from the city of Megara (MEH-guh-ruh) in Greece.
pages.brief: Long ago, Byzas leads a group of people from Megara in Greece toward the area that becomes Istanbul. The city sits as an important port on the water road between two seas, with travelers from East and West arriving by boat.

pages.text: Istanbul has had many rulers and has been a capital of many empires. Its name has changed several times. It became Istanbul in 1930. Many buildings and parts of the city have been destroyed and built again. Let’s visit some interesting places in Istanbul. Istanbul’s Other Names Long ago, Istanbul was called Byzantium (bih-ZAN-tee-uhm) for a leader named Byzas. Later, it was called Constantinople for a ruler named Constantine the Great.
pages.brief: Over time, different rulers govern Istanbul, and parts of the city are destroyed and rebuilt. Old buildings stand beside newer ones, showing the city’s many changes. Long ago it was called Byzantium for Byzas, and later Constantinople for Constantine the Great.

pages.text: Water Tank This huge underground water tank is no longer used. Long ago, it was the most important water supply for the city. The water came from a lake. Istanbul has many very old water tanks. This one is the biggest.
pages.brief: A huge underground water tank stretches out with many tall columns holding up its ceiling. Long ago, water from a lake filled it and supplied the city. It is no longer used, but it is the biggest of Istanbul’s many very old water tanks.

pages.text: Covered Market This huge covered market is made of stone. The first parts were built in 1461, and other parts were added over time. Today, it has sixty-one covered streets and more than four thousand shops. Shops sell clothing, jewelry, rugs, and many other things. Wowser! • More than 250,000 people shop at this market every day. • More than 20,000 people work there every day. • In 2014, more people visited this market than any other place in the world. That year, more than 91 million people came.
pages.brief: A huge stone-covered market spreads through many covered streets, with more than four thousand shops selling clothing, jewelry, rugs, and other goods. Crowds of shoppers and workers fill the market, which began in 1461 and grew over time.

pages.text: Island Tower This tower is on a small island in Istanbul’s waterway. It was built about 2,400 years ago. Long ago, people used the tower to watch ships passing by. Later, the tower was a lighthouse. Today, it is a restaurant. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A tower stands on a small island in Istanbul’s waterway. Long ago, people used it to watch ships passing by, and later it served as a lighthouse. Today, the tower is a restaurant, with water all around the little island.

pages.text: Tall Tower This tall tower was built in 1348. The tower was first used as a lighthouse. Later, it was a prison. Then, people used it to watch for fires. Today, people visit the tower to look out over Istanbul.
pages.brief: A tall stone tower rises above Istanbul. Built in 1348, it was first a lighthouse, later a prison, and then a place to watch for fires. Today, visitors go up the tower to look out over the city.

pages.text: Huge Palace This palace was built in the late 1400s. Rulers lived here for almost four hundred years. They added new parts to the palace. In 1924, it became a museum. The palace has three big gates and four outdoor spaces with gardens. High walls are all around the outside.
pages.brief: A huge palace with high walls around the outside stands in Istanbul. Built in the late 1400s, rulers lived there for almost four hundred years and added new parts. It has three big gates and four outdoor garden spaces. In 1924, it became a museum.

pages.text: Grand Museum This huge building was first built as a church in the year 360. When it was built, it was the biggest building in the world. It burned down two times and was built again. It became a mosque in the year 1453. Later, it became a museum. Today, it is a mosque again.
pages.brief: A huge building stands in Istanbul, first built as a church in the year 360 and once the biggest building in the world. It burned down two times and was rebuilt. It became a mosque, later a museum, and today it is a mosque again.

pages.text: City Square This square was built in the 1700s. All of Istanbul’s water lines met here. Today, the square has shops, hotels, and restaurants. Parades and New Year’s celebrations take place here.
pages.brief: A city square in Istanbul is filled with shops, hotels, and restaurants. Built in the 1700s, it was once the place where all of Istanbul’s water lines met. Today, parades and New Year’s celebrations take place there.

pages.text: A Trip Back in Time Istanbul is a big city with an interesting history. It brings two continents together and has many wonderful places to visit. Each part of Istanbul has a story to tell. Going there is like taking a trip back in time.
pages.brief: A broad view of Istanbul brings together the city’s two continents, its waterways, and its many wonderful places to visit. The big city has an interesting history, and each part has a story to tell. Going there is like taking a trip back in time.

books.title: The Secret Lives of Snails and Slugs
books.art_why: Non-fiction science about real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Can you guess what walks on one slimy foot? Here’s another clue: this animal has a tongue covered with sharp teeth. Believe it or not, the right answer is a snail or slug. You’ll be amazed when you discover more about these creepy crawlers!
pages.brief: A snail and a slug are shown close together, one gliding on its single slimy foot. A tongue covered with sharp teeth is visible, while the animal moves along, as if asking what walks on one foot.

pages.text: Snail and Slug Bodies Snails and slugs are much alike. They belong to the family of animals called mollusks. The mollusk family also includes clams, squids, and octopuses. All mollusks have soft bodies and no backbones, and most have shells to protect their bodies. Even slugs have a tiny shell hidden beneath their skin. Ruffle-back snail Snail with spiral-shaped shell.
pages.brief: A ruffle-back snail with a spiral-shaped shell rests beside a slug. Around them, clams, a squid and an octopus represent the mollusk family: soft-bodied animals without backbones, most with shells for protection, while the slug’s tiny shell is hidden beneath its skin.

pages.text: SNAIL eyespots tentacles foot breathing pore mouth tentacles with eyes at the tips SLUG mantle breathing pore head sensory tentacles foot slime gland mouth Snails and slugs are also called gastropods, which means “belly foot.” A snail or slug has one foot, with its head at one end. It seems to walk on its belly, but actually it is crawling on its foot. Snails and slugs have tongues with many rows of tiny sharp teeth.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug are shown side by side so their body parts can be compared. The snail has a shell, eyespots on tentacle tips, a breathing pore, mouth and foot; the slug shows its mantle, head, sensory tentacles, slime gland, foot and mouth.

pages.text: Snails and slugs have four tentacles shaped like arms. At the ends of the top two tentacles are the eyes. These top tentacles are also used to smell. Slugs and snails use their bottom two tentacles for feeling their way along.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug are shown feeling their way forward. Each has four arm-shaped tentacles: the top two tentacles carry eyes at the tips and also smell the air, while the bottom two tentacles stretch out to feel the ground and nearby surfaces.

pages.text: Slime Snails and slugs move very slowly, gliding along on their single feet. The foot produces slime that helps the snail crawl, like sliding on a bed of jelly. The goo is sticky, so it also helps the animal climb. Slugs and snails drink through their skin, and their slime filters the water.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug glide slowly on their single feet over a wet surface. Their feet produce sticky slime, like a bed of jelly, helping them crawl and climb. Water touches their skin, which they drink through, with the slime filtering the water.

pages.text: Slime also helps protect snails and slugs. Birds, snakes, crabs, turtles, and other animals eat snails and slugs. But the slime makes it difficult for these hunters because dinner gets very sticky. Slug slime also tastes awful. This disgusting goo helps stop animals from eating snails and slugs.
pages.brief: A bird, a snake, a crab and a turtle approach a snail and a slug as hunters. The snail and slug are covered in sticky slime that makes them difficult to eat; the slug’s awful-tasting goo discourages the animals from taking a bite.

pages.text: Kinds of Snails and Slugs The first snails and slugs probably lived around 600 million years ago. Today, there are around 80,000 kinds of snails and slugs. Some snails and slugs live on land, and others live in water. Many beautiful slugs and snails live in the ocean. Both land and water snails and slugs love wetness. If a snail or slug dries out, it will die.
pages.brief: Snails and slugs are shown in many kinds and places: some on land, some in water, and many colorful ones in the ocean. They love wetness, and a snail or slug drying out would die. The first kinds probably lived around 600 million years ago.

pages.text: Snails and slugs can be as tiny as the period on this page, and the largest are the size of rabbits! Snails can have dull, bright, spotted, or striped shells. Many sea slugs are brightly colored with red, blue, purple, silver, or yellow. Most land slugs are brown or green. One slug looks quite a bit like a fruit. It is the banana slug, which lives in the western United States. A banana slug is yellow with black spots, and it can grow as big as a banana.
pages.brief: A tiny snail and a huge snail the size of a rabbit show the range of sizes. Shells are dull, bright, spotted or striped. Sea slugs display red, blue, purple, silver or yellow, while a yellow banana slug with black spots rests on the ground.

pages.text: The Lives of Snails and Slugs Like bears, land snails and slugs sleep through cold winters. Snails nap in their shells, and slugs sleep in holes they’ve dug in the dirt. In the spring, they come out. They’re very hungry after they wake up, and they need to find plants to eat.
pages.brief: In cold winter, a land snail naps inside its shell while a slug sleeps in a hole dug in the dirt. When spring arrives, both come out very hungry and search for plants to eat.

pages.text: Snails and slugs spend most of their time searching for food. Land snails and slugs eat live plants, and some eat dead plants, too. They rub their tongues on leaves and stems. Sharp teeth on their tongues grind off bits of plants. Sea snails and slugs eat underwater plants, sponges, and tiny ocean animals.
pages.brief: A land snail and slug search for food, rubbing their tooth-covered tongues on leaves and stems to grind off bits of plants. Some also eat dead plants. Underwater, a sea snail and sea slug feed on underwater plants, sponges and tiny ocean animals.

pages.text: Almost all snails and slugs lay eggs. When each egg hatches, a baby snail or slug crawls out. How long does a snail or slug live? It depends on the type and size. Small snails and slugs usually live about six months, and large snails and slugs might live eight to ten years.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug are shown with eggs. When each egg hatches, a baby snail or slug crawls out. Small snails and slugs usually live about six months, while large ones might live eight to ten years.

pages.text: Slugs help turn dead plants into soil. Conclusion Some snails and slugs can damage crops and gardens, but snails and slugs are very important. They clean up the world by eating dead plants. They provide a source of food for birds and other animals. Now you know all about the secret lives of snails and slugs! Do You Know? Many people love to eat snails cooked in butter and garlic. In some areas, snails are served in soup or salads.
pages.brief: A slug moves through dead plants, helping turn them into soil. Birds nearby may eat snails and slugs. Some snails damage crops and gardens, but they are important cleaners and food. Cooked snails with butter and garlic are shown as food people enjoy.
